title: Cost Optimisation

techniques.name: Model Routing and Tiering
techniques.q: Does this request need the big model?
techniques.what: Send each request, and each step of a pipeline, to the cheapest model that can handle it. At run time, a router judges difficulty up front, or a cascade tries a small model first and escalates only when a check fails or confidence is low. At design time, evaluate each pipeline step on its own test set and give it the cheapest tier that meets its bar. Errors compound across steps, so spend on the weakest one.
use: High-volume traffic with a mix of easy and hard requests
Multi-step pipelines whose steps differ in difficulty, such as classify, extract, assess and draft
Latency-sensitive paths where small models also answer faster
metrics: task type, input length or tenant → model
a classifier predicts which model is needed (e.g. RouteLLM)
small model first; escalate on low confidence or a failed check
each pipeline step gets the cheapest tier that passes its own eval set
end-to-end accuracy ≈ the product of step accuracies, so the weakest step limits all
cost per task at an equal success rate
steps: Label a sample of real traffic and write a small eval set for each pipeline step
Run steps on each tier; pick the cheapest that meets the bar, spending on the weakest step
Route requests with simple rules first, then a trained router once you have outcome data
Add escalation on failed checks, and recheck tiers when models change
pitfalls: Misrouted hard tasks fail on the weak model, so measure quality per route
Measuring only end to end hides the weak step
Cascades add latency every time they escalate
techniques.remember: Smallest model that passes, per request and per step. Escalate on doubt.
techniques.cap: Example assumes the small model costs 1/20 of the large one: 0.2 × 1 + 0.8 × 0.05 = 0.24.

techniques.name: Prompt Caching
techniques.q: Am I paying again for the same prompt prefix?
techniques.what: Providers can store the processed form of a long, unchanging prompt prefix, such as the system prompt, tool definitions and reference documents, and reuse it on the next call. Cached input is billed at a fraction of the normal price and is processed faster. A separate response cache can skip the model entirely for repeated questions.
use: Agents that resend the same system prompt and tools on every step
Chat over a fixed document, codebase or knowledge pack
Many users sharing one long instruction set
metrics: the longest stable prefix: system prompt, tools, documents, earlier turns
cached input tokens ÷ total input tokens
cached reads cost a fraction of normal input
providers require a minimum prefix, often around 1,024 tokens
minutes by default, refreshed on each hit
reuse whole answers for near-duplicate questions
steps: Order the prompt: static content first, variable content (user message, date) last
Mark the cache breakpoint where your provider requires it, or rely on automatic caching
Keep timestamps, request IDs and shuffled examples out of the prefix
Watch hit rate. A sudden drop usually means something changed in the prefix
pitfalls: One changed character early in the prompt invalidates everything after it
Cache writes can cost more than normal input on some providers
Semantic caches can serve a stale or wrong answer to a subtly different question
techniques.cap: Units = base input price per token. Uses Anthropic’s published multipliers: cache write 1.25×, cache read 0.1×.

techniques.name: Prompt & Tool Controls
techniques.q: Is the agent using more tokens and calls than it needs?
techniques.what: Put limits and lean defaults on what each request can consume: concise system prompts, capped output length, fewer and tighter tool definitions, compact tool results, and a cap on how many steps an agent loop can take. Agents are expensive mostly because they loop and carry bulky tool output from step to step.
use: Agent loops with many tool calls per task
Tools that return large payloads: search results, logs, full records
Prompts that grew over time with duplicated instructions
metrics: maximum iterations or tool calls per task
expose only the tools relevant to this task
return IDs and summaries, not full payloads
remove duplicated rules and unused examples
a JSON schema instead of verbose prose
steps: Measure tokens per step and find the biggest contributors
Set max_tokens and a step budget per task type, with a graceful stop
Load tool definitions dynamically so each call carries only what it needs
Trim tool responses at the source: paginate, filter fields, summarize
pitfalls: Caps set too low truncate answers or stop tasks halfway
Cutting examples can quietly lower quality, so re-run your evals
Dynamic tool loading adds a selection step that can choose wrong
techniques.remember: Budget every loop. Trim every payload.
techniques.cap: Each block is one step, sized by its tokens. Controls cut both the number of steps and their size.

techniques.name: Context Pruning
techniques.q: Does the model need everything in the context window?
techniques.what: Long-running agents pile up history, tool output and retrieved documents, and every token is paid for again on every turn. Pruning keeps the context small: summarize old turns, drop tool results once they have been used, retrieve fewer and better chunks, and compress prompts.
use: Long conversations and multi-hour agent sessions
Agents that read large files, logs or web pages
RAG pipelines that stuff many chunks into every prompt
metrics: keep the last N turns word for word
older turns become a running summary
drop raw outputs once they have been used
fewer, re-ranked chunks instead of the top 20
store facts outside the context and retrieve on demand
steps: Plot context size per turn for your longest sessions
Summarize when context crosses a threshold, keeping decisions and open tasks
Clear bulky tool outputs after extracting what matters
Re-run long-task evals to confirm nothing important was lost
pitfalls: Summaries drop details the agent needs later
Aggressive pruning breaks references to earlier turns
Pruning changes the prompt prefix, which can cancel prompt-cache savings
techniques.remember: Every token is paid for on every turn.
techniques.cap: Totals are the sum of context size over 21 turns in this example. Summarizing at 16k keeps each turn cheap.

cmp.best: Can drop details the agent needs

techniques.name: Request Scheduling
techniques.q: Does this have to run now, and at full speed?
techniques.what: Control when and how requests reach the model: queue them, merge identical requests already in flight, rate-limit per user, and move non-urgent work to quiet hours or cheaper service tiers. Smoother load also lets you size reserved capacity near the average instead of the peak.
use: Mixed workloads: interactive chat plus reports, indexing, enrichment
Provisioned or reserved capacity you pay for by the hour
Multi-tenant products that need fair use and spend limits
metrics: run reports and indexing when demand is low
lower-priority tiers at a discount, where offered
reserved throughput sized to smoothed load
steps: Tag every request as interactive, near-real-time or background
Send background work through a queue with retries and backoff
Set per-tenant quotas and alerts on spend
Review utilization regularly and right-size reserved capacity
pitfalls: Queued work adds delay, so keep interactive paths separate
Retries without backoff multiply cost during outages
Hard quotas can block legitimate spikes; allow controlled bursts
techniques.remember: Urgent now. Everything else when it’s cheap.
techniques.cap: Same total work, lower peak. Reserved capacity only has to cover the peak.

techniques.name: Batch Processing
techniques.q: Can this wait a few hours for half the price?
techniques.what: Submit large sets of non-urgent requests as one asynchronous batch. Major providers price batch jobs at about half the standard rate and return results within 24 hours, often much sooner. Ideal for evaluations, classification, enrichment and summaries over large datasets.
use: Nightly or weekly jobs nobody waits on
Running eval suites and backfills
Tagging, extraction or summarization over large archives
metrics: about 50% off standard pricing on major providers
a file of requests, each with a custom ID
can combine with prompt caching for further savings
steps: Find workloads nobody waits on: nightly jobs, evals, backfills
Write requests to a JSONL file with a custom ID per item
Submit, poll for completion, and match results back by ID
Retry only the failed items in a follow-up batch
pitfalls: No streaming and no real-time answers
Partial failures must be tracked by ID
Very large jobs hit size and rate limits, so split them
techniques.remember: Not urgent? Batch it and pay half.
techniques.cap: Check your provider’s current batch pricing and limits.

techniques.name: Semantic Response Caching
techniques.q: Has someone already asked this, in other words?
techniques.what: Store whole answers keyed by the meaning of the question. Each new question is embedded and compared with cached questions; if one is similar enough, in the same scope and not expired, its stored answer is returned and the model is never called. This differs from prompt caching, where the provider reuses a processed prompt prefix but the model still writes a fresh answer. The risks are false hits (a similar but different question gets the wrong answer), stale answers after the source changes, and personal answers leaking between users.
use: High-volume support bots where many users ask the same FAQ in different words
Answers that depend only on shared content, such as plans, policies and how-to steps
Traffic where a lookup is far cheaper and faster than an LLM call
metrics: how close a question must be to reuse an answer; lower means more hits and more false hits
global, per tenant or per user; personalised answers are never shared
FAQ-like intents only; account-specific and live-data intents bypass the cache
how long an entry lives before it must be regenerated
purge or version entries when the source document changes
hit rate, false-hit rate from sampled reviews, and ₹ saved net of lookups
steps: Classify intents and send account-specific or live-data questions straight to the model
Pick a threshold from a labelled set of paraphrase and near-miss pairs, not by feel
Tag every entry with its scope and the version of the source it came from
Sample hits for review, track false-hit rate and ₹ saved, and purge on source changes
pitfalls: A loose threshold returns confident answers to different questions: “roaming in UAE” is not “roaming in USA”
A global cache holding account answers shows one customer’s data to another
A long TTL keeps serving old prices after the tariff changes
techniques.remember: Cache the shared answers, never the personal ones. Tune the threshold on near misses.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Tarang Mobile, a fictional telecom operator, with 1,00,000 questions a day, a 0.90 threshold, a global FAQ cache and account intents excluded.

cmp.needs: Medium: vector store, intent filter, reviews

techniques.name: Cost Attribution and Budget Guards
techniques.q: Which feature, customer or run is spending the money, and what stops a runaway?
techniques.what: The other techniques in this module lower the price of each call; this one makes spend visible and bounded. Every LLM call is tagged with who and what it serves (team, feature, customer, agent run, model), usually at a gateway, so the bill can be split by any tag and unit costs such as ₹ per invoice or per resolved ticket can be tracked. The same tags drive guards: a token or rupee budget per agent run that stops a looping agent, daily caps per customer or API key, alerts at a share of budget, and anomaly detection on spend per tag. Hard stops need care: a cap on a whole feature or on the account can halt real work for everyone.
use: Agent products where one run can loop for hours
Multi-tenant SaaS with free tiers or usage-based pricing
Finance asking which features and customers the LLM bill belongs to
metrics: share of spend with team, feature, customer and run tags; aim above 95%
₹ per business outcome: per invoice drafted, per ticket resolved
tokens, rupees or steps per agent run, with a graceful stop
daily or monthly limits per tenant or API key
alerts at 50/80/100% of budget; spikes by tag against a baseline
legitimate work halted by caps set at too coarse a level
steps: Route all LLM calls through one gateway or SDK wrapper that requires tags
Report spend by feature, customer and run, and set unit-cost targets
Add per-run budgets and per-customer caps with clear user messages
Alert on budget thresholds and anomalies; review the top spenders weekly
pitfalls: Calls made directly to the provider that skip the gateway and its tags
A single account-wide hard cap that takes the whole product down
Budgets set in tokens while prices differ several-fold between models
techniques.remember: Tag every call; guard each run and each customer, not the whole account.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Vyapar Sathi, a fictional small-business SaaS, spends about ₹8,00,000 a month on LLM calls.

cmp.best: Coarse hard caps halt real work

chooser: Most requests are simple, but everything runs on the top model

Route easy traffic to a small model and escalate only when checks fail.
Every call resends the same long system prompt and tool list
caching
Put the stable prefix first so the provider bills it at the cached rate.
Agent loops run long and outputs are wordy
controls
Cap output, set a step budget, and trim tools and tool results.
Long conversations get slower and pricier every turn
pruning
Summarize old turns and clear used tool output once context crosses a threshold.
Traffic spikes force us to pay for peak capacity
scheduling
Queue background work, shift it off-peak, and set quotas per tenant.
We process large datasets that nobody waits on
batch
Submit them through a batch API at about half the price.
Thousands of users ask the same FAQ in different words and each one pays for a fresh LLM answer
semcache
Put a semantic cache in front of the model for FAQ intents only, tune the threshold on near-miss pairs, and purge entries when the source changes.
Nobody knows which feature or customer drives the LLM bill, or an agent loop ran up a large charge
costattr
Tag every call at a gateway, report unit costs, and add per-run budgets, per-customer caps and anomaly alerts.

import json
from litellm import completion

SMALL = "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5"     # tried on 500 labelled requests   #@1
LARGE = "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5"    # swap in your current models      #@1
HARD_INTENTS = {"tax", "portfolio", "complaint"}                            #@2

def route(intent: str) -> str:                                              #@2
    return LARGE if intent in HARD_INTENTS else SMALL                       #@2

def valid(text: str) -> bool:                                               #@3
    try:
        out = json.loads(text)                                              #@3
    except ValueError:
        return False                                                        #@3
    return bool(out.get("answer")) and out.get("confidence", 0) >= 0.7      #@3

def ask(model: str, q: str) -> str:
    prompt = q + '\nReply as JSON: {"answer": ..., "confidence": 0-1}'
    r = completion(model=model, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return r.choices[0].message.content

def answer(q: str, intent: str) -> str:
    model = route(intent)                                                   #@2
    text = ask(model, q)                                                    #@3
    if model == SMALL and not valid(text):          # cascade               #@4
        model, text = LARGE, ask(LARGE, q)                                  #@4
    log_route(intent, model, cost=COST[model], ok=valid(text))              #@5,6
    return text
steps: Label a traffic sample
Run the small model on a few hundred real, labelled requests. Here it passes 8 of 10, so most traffic doesn’t need the large model.
Route with simple rules first
Start with rules on intent or length: FAQs and extraction go to the small model, tax and complaints to the large one.
Validate the cheap answers
A validator checks every small-model answer: valid JSON, a non-empty answer, confidence of at least 0.7. One of eight fails.
Escalate what fails
The failed answer is re-asked on the large model. This cascade trades a little latency on escalations for safety.
Count the cost
The small model costs 1/20 as much. Eight small calls plus three large ones: (8 × 0.05 + 3 × 1) ÷ 10 = 34% of all-large spend.
Track quality per route
Log cost and pass rate for every route. If a route’s pass rate drops, tighten the rules or train a learned router on the logs.

import datetime, anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
TOOLS = load_tool_definitions()                  # 1,500 tokens, never changes   #@1
REPORT = open("annual_report.txt").read()        # 10,000 tokens, never changes  #@1

def ask(question: str):
    return client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=1024,       # use your current model
        tools=TOOLS,                                      # cached first           #@1
        system=[
            {"type": "text", "text": "You are an equity research assistant."},   #@1
            {"type": "text", "text": REPORT,
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},    # breakpoint: cache up to here   #@2
        ],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
                   f"Today is {datetime.date.today()}. {question}"}],   # variable part last   #@1,5
    )

r1 = ask("Summarize segment revenue.")
print(r1.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens)      # 12,000 written at 1.25x   #@3
r2 = ask("List the key risks.")                  # within 5 minutes          #@4
print(r2.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)          # 12,000 read at 0.1x       #@4

u = r2.usage                                                                 #@6
cached = u.cache_read_input_tokens                                           #@6
total = cached + u.cache_creation_input_tokens + u.input_tokens              #@6
print(f"hit rate {cached / total:.0%}")          # alert if this drops       #@6
steps: Order the prompt
Caching works on the prefix, in the order tools, system, messages. Put everything that never changes first and the question last.
Mark the breakpoint
cache_control marks the end of the stable prefix. Everything up to it, 12,000 tokens here, is cached for 5 minutes by default.
The first call writes the cache
Call 1 processes the prefix and stores it. The write costs 1.25× the normal input price, slightly more than no caching.
The next call reads it
Call 2 arrives within 5 minutes with an identical prefix, so the 12,000 tokens bill at 0.1×. Only the question is new.
One changed byte breaks it
The date is safe in the user message. Move it into the system text above the breakpoint and every call misses and rewrites.
Monitor the hit rate

import json, anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MAX_STEPS = 6                                                          #@5
TOOLS_BY_TASK = {"kyc": ["read_page", "extract_fields", "flag_mismatch"]}   #@2

def trim(result: dict) -> str:                                         #@4
    keep = {k: result[k] for k in ("pan", "name", "dob", "page") if k in result}   #@4
    return json.dumps(keep)                  # fields, not the raw OCR text   #@4

def run(task_type: str, messages: list):
    tools = [ALL_TOOLS[n] for n in TOOLS_BY_TASK[task_type]]           #@2
    for step in range(MAX_STEPS):                                      #@5
        resp = client.messages.create(
            model=MODEL, max_tokens=400,                               #@3
            system=SYSTEM + " Reply with the JSON fields only.",       #@3
            tools=tools, messages=messages)
        log_usage(task_type, step, resp.usage)   # tokens per step          #@1,6
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return resp                          # finished within budget
        messages += [{"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content},
                     {"role": "user", "content": run_tools(resp, post=trim)}]   #@4
    return stop_gracefully(messages, reason="step budget reached")     #@5

# Nightly: rerun the KYC eval set, compare tokens per task and pass rate   #@6
steps: Measure tokens per step
Log usage on every step. This KYC task takes 8 steps and 52k tokens, and each step is bigger than the last because context accumulates.

Cap and shape the output
Set max_tokens per task type and ask for JSON fields instead of prose. Replies fall from about 900 tokens to 250.
Trim tool results at the source
The page reader returned 3,000 tokens of raw OCR text. Return only the fields the next step needs: about 600 tokens.
Set a step budget with a graceful stop
Cap the loop at 6 steps. If the budget runs out, return a partial result for review instead of looping on.

import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")
LIMIT, KEEP_RECENT = 16_000, 4                                        #@2,3

def tokens(msgs: list) -> int:                                        #@1
    return sum(len(enc.encode(m["content"])) for m in msgs)           #@1

def clear_used_tool_results(msgs: list) -> list:                      #@5
    for m in msgs[:-1]:                                               #@5
        if m.get("is_tool_result") and m.get("values_recorded"):      #@5
            m["content"] = "[tool output cleared; key values recorded]"   #@5
    return msgs

def prune(history: list) -> list:
    history = clear_used_tool_results(history)                       #@5
    if tokens(history) <= LIMIT:                                      #@2
        return history
    old, recent = history[:-KEEP_RECENT], history[-KEEP_RECENT:]      #@3
    note = llm("Summarize decisions, client facts, figures and open tasks:\n"   #@4
               + "\n".join(m["content"] for m in old))                #@4
    return [{"role": "user", "content": "Summary so far: " + note}] + recent   #@4

# Eval: replay 30 day-long sessions; check answers that need early facts   #@6
steps: Plot context per turn
Every turn resends the whole history. Context here grows by about 1.9k tokens a turn and reaches 40k by turn 20.
Set a threshold
Decide when to act: once context passes 16k tokens, prune before the next call.
Keep recent turns word for word
The last 4 turns stay verbatim, because the next reply usually depends on them.
Summarize the older turns
Everything older becomes a short note that keeps decisions, client facts, figures and open tasks. Context drops back and grows again.
Clear used tool output
Raw statement extracts are replaced by a placeholder once their key figures have been recorded in a reply.
Check nothing was lost
Replay long sessions and test questions that need early facts. Input paid over turns 0–20 falls from 441k to 190k tokens.

import hashlib, random, redis
from celery import Celery
from celery.schedules import crontab
app = Celery("llm", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0")
r = redis.Redis()

app.conf.task_routes = {"tasks.chat": {"queue": "interactive"},       #@1,2
                        "tasks.summarize": {"queue": "background"}}    #@1,2

@app.task(bind=True, max_retries=5, rate_limit="100/m")               #@4
def summarize(self, client_id: str, note: str):
    key = "dedup:" + hashlib.sha256(note.encode()).hexdigest()         #@3
    if not r.set(key, 1, nx=True, ex=86_400):  # same note in flight or done   #@3
        return "duplicate skipped"                                     #@3
    try:
        return llm_summarize(note)
    except RateLimitError as exc:                                      #@4
        r.delete(key)
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=2 ** self.request.retries + random.random())   #@4

app.conf.beat_schedule = {"nightly-notes": {                          #@5
    "task": "tasks.enqueue_notes", "schedule": crontab(hour=0, minute=30)}}   #@5

# celery -A tasks worker -Q interactive --concurrency 32   (reserved)    #@2,6
# celery -A tasks worker -Q background  --concurrency 6    (capped)      #@2,6
steps: Tag every request
Label each call interactive, near-real-time or background. Chat is interactive; end-of-day contract-note summaries are background.
Give each class its own queue
Separate queues and worker pools mean a bulk job can never sit in front of a customer’s chat message.
Drop duplicates
The same note is often enqueued twice by a retry or a double click. A Redis key with SET NX skips work already in flight or done.
Retry with backoff and jitter
On a 429, wait 1 s, 2 s, 4 s… plus a random fraction. Immediate retries during an outage multiply load and cost.
Move background work off-peak
The nightly job starts at 00:30, when chat traffic is lowest, instead of at 16:00 on top of the afternoon load.
Right-size reserved capacity
The peak falls from 11 units to the interactive peak of 8, so reserved capacity shrinks and utilization rises from 43% to 59%.

import json, time
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

with open("tickets.jsonl", "w") as f:                              #@1,2
    for t in tickets:                                              #@2
        f.write(json.dumps({"custom_id": t.id, "method": "POST",   #@2
            "url": "/v1/chat/completions",                         #@2
            "body": {"model": "gpt-4o-mini", "max_tokens": 200,
                     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT + t.text}]}}) + "\n")

upload = client.files.create(file=open("tickets.jsonl", "rb"), purpose="batch")   #@3
batch = client.batches.create(input_file_id=upload.id,             #@3
                              endpoint="/v1/chat/completions",
                              completion_window="24h")             #@3
while (b := client.batches.retrieve(batch.id)).status not in (
        "completed", "failed", "expired", "cancelled"):            #@3
    time.sleep(300)                                                #@3

for line in client.files.content(b.output_file_id).text.splitlines():   #@4
    r = json.loads(line)                                           #@4
    save(r["custom_id"], r["response"]["body"]["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])   #@4

failed = [json.loads(l)["custom_id"] for l in                      #@5
          client.files.content(b.error_file_id).text.splitlines()] if b.error_file_id else []   #@5
resubmit(failed)                        # a small follow-up batch     #@5
# Bill check: batch requests are billed at 50% of standard rates   #@6
steps: Find work nobody waits on
Nightly tagging and eval suites fit; live chat and agent loops that need each answer immediately do not.
Write one request per line
Each line of the JSONL file is a complete request with a unique custom_id, so results can be matched later.
Upload, submit and poll
Create the batch with a 24-hour completion window, then poll every few minutes. Many batches finish much sooner.
Match results by ID
Results are not guaranteed to come back in input order. Join each one to its ticket by custom_id.
Retry only what failed
The error file lists the failed IDs. Resubmit just those in a small follow-up batch, never the whole job.
Check the bill

from redisvl.extensions.cache.llm import SemanticCache
from redisvl.query.filter import Tag

ACCOUNT = {"bill", "balance", "recharge_status", "sim_block"}   # never cached   #@1

cache = SemanticCache(
    name="tarang_faq",
    redis_url="redis://localhost:6379",
    distance_threshold=0.10,          # cosine distance 0.10 = similarity 0.90   #@2
    ttl=24 * 3600,                    # entries expire after 24 hours            #@4
    filterable_fields=[{"name": "scope", "type": "tag"},                         #@3
                       {"name": "tariff_v", "type": "tag"}],                     #@5
)

def answer(question: str, user: dict) -> str:
    if classify_intent(question) in ACCOUNT:          # live, personal data     #@1
        return llm_answer(question, user=user)        # straight to the model   #@1
    tariff_v = current_tariff_version()               # e.g. "2026-09"          #@5
    only = (Tag("scope") == "global") & (Tag("tariff_v") == tariff_v)          #@3,5
    hits = cache.check(prompt=question, filter_expression=only, num_results=1)  #@2
    if hits:
        log_hit(question, hits[0]["prompt"], float(hits[0]["vector_distance"]))  #@6
        return hits[0]["response"]                    # no LLM call              #@2,6
    reply = llm_answer(question, user=None)           # shared facts only        #@3,4
    cache.store(prompt=question, response=reply,                                 #@4
                filters={"scope": "global", "tariff_v": tariff_v})              #@4,5
    log_miss(question)                                                           #@6
    return reply
steps: Keep personal questions out

40,000 of Tarang Mobile's 1,00,000 daily questions are about a customer's own bill, balance or SIM. Their answers depend on live, personal data, so they go straight to the model and are never looked up or stored.
Set the threshold on near misses

RedisVL measures cosine distance, so distance_threshold 0.10 means similarity 0.90. “How do I turn on roaming?” and “activate roaming?” score 0.94 and rightly share an answer. “Roaming packs for UAE” and “Roaming packs for USA” can score 0.91 and must not. Choose the threshold from labelled paraphrase and near-miss pairs.
Scope the cache

Every entry is tagged scope=global and the lookup filters on that tag. Only shared answers are stored, and they are generated without the user's details, so one customer's answer can never be served to another.
Store on a miss, with a TTL
On a miss the model answers and the reply is stored with a 24-hour TTL. The next paraphrase within a day is a hit; after 24 hours the entry expires and is written again.
Invalidate when the source changes

Each entry carries the tariff version it was written under. When the tariff page changes mid-week the version bumps, old entries stop matching at once, and the next question gets a fresh answer. Relying on the 24-hour TTL alone would serve about 5,610 stale price answers.
Measure hits, false hits and ₹

Log every hit with its distance and sample hits for human review. At 0.90 the cache answers 45,600 questions a day, about 720 of them false hits. At ₹0.40 per LLM answer and ₹0.01 per lookup on the 60,000 FAQ questions, it saves ₹18,240 − ₹600 = ₹17,640 a day.

from openai import OpenAI

gw = OpenAI(base_url="https://llm-gw.internal/v1", api_key=TEAM_VIRTUAL_KEY)   # LiteLLM proxy  #@1

def call(messages, *, feature, customer, run):
    run.check_budget()                               # raises before overspending  #@3
    r = gw.chat.completions.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5", messages=messages, user=customer,
        extra_body={"metadata": {"tags": [f"feature:{feature}",                       #@1
                                           f"customer:{customer}", f"run:{run.id}"]}})
    run.add(r.usage)                                 # ₹ from tokens × price        #@3
    return r

class RunBudget:
    def __init__(self, rid, max_inr=50): self.id, self.max, self.spent = rid, max_inr, 0.0
    def add(self, u): self.spent += inr(u.prompt_tokens, u.completion_tokens)
    def check_budget(self):
        if self.spent >= self.max: raise BudgetExceeded(self.id)   # stop the loop   #@3

# per-customer cap: POST /key/generate {"max_budget": 500, "budget_duration": "1d"}  #@4
# daily job: spend by tag → ₹ per invoice; alert at 80%; flag 3× spikes           #@2,5

steps: Send every call through a gateway with tags
Vyapar Sathi, a fictional small-business SaaS, routes all LLM calls through a LiteLLM proxy. Each call carries feature, customer and run tags, and calls without tags are rejected.
Report spend by tag
The bill of about ₹8,00,000 a month splits into GST invoice drafting 46%, the support agent 31%, reconciliation runs 15% and one free-tier customer 8%. Invoice drafting costs ₹1.40 per invoice.
Budget each agent run
A reconciliation run may spend ₹50. When a run loops, it stops with a clear message instead of running all night. Runaway loops had cost ₹1,20,000 a month.
Cap each customer
Each customer key has a daily budget. A free-tier account that scripted thousands of requests had cost ₹80,000 a month; its cap now stops it at ₹500 a day.
Alert and detect spikes
Alerts fire at 80% of a budget, and a daily job flags any tag whose spend is three times its usual level.
Review the top spenders
Each week the team reads the ten most expensive runs and customers. Waste falls from ₹2,00,000 to about ₹14,000 a month, with about 40 real runs stopped early.

from litellm import completion

SMALL = "openai/gpt-4o-mini"                     # swap in your current models
LARGE = "anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022"
HARD = ("tax", "portfolio", "compare", "why did")

def pick(q: str) -> str:
    return LARGE if len(q) > 400 or any(w in q.lower() for w in HARD) else SMALL

def ask(model: str, q: str) -> str:
    out = completion(model=model, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": q}])
    return out.choices[0].message.content

def answer(q: str) -> str:
    model = pick(q)
    text = ask(model, q)
    if model == SMALL and not passes_checks(text):   # cascade: escalate on failure
        text = ask(LARGE, q)
    return text

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

report = open("annual_report.txt").read()          # large and unchanging

def ask(question: str):
    return client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5",                  # use your current model
        max_tokens=1024,
        system=[
            {"type": "text", "text": "You are an equity research assistant."},
            {"type": "text", "text": report,
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},   # cache everything up to here
        ],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],   # variable part last
    )

code:
from redisvl.extensions.cache.llm import SemanticCache
from redisvl.query.filter import Tag

ACCOUNT_INTENTS = {"bill", "balance", "recharge_status", "sim_block"}

cache = SemanticCache(
    name="tarang_faq",
    redis_url="redis://localhost:6379",
    distance_threshold=0.10,            # cosine distance: similarity >= 0.90
    ttl=24 * 3600,                      # seconds
    filterable_fields=[{"name": "scope", "type": "tag"},
                       {"name": "tariff_v", "type": "tag"}],
)


def answer(question: str, user: dict) -> str:
    if classify_intent(question) in ACCOUNT_INTENTS:
        return llm_answer(question, user=user)          # personal: never cached
    version = current_tariff_version()
    only = (Tag("scope") == "global") & (Tag("tariff_v") == version)
    hits = cache.check(prompt=question, filter_expression=only, num_results=1)
    if hits:
        return hits[0]["response"]
    reply = llm_answer(question, user=None)             # shared facts only
    cache.store(prompt=question, response=reply,
                filters={"scope": "global", "tariff_v": version})
    return reply

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

# Labelled pairs: True = same answer is correct, False = near miss
PAIRS = [
    ("How do I activate international roaming?", "activate roaming kaise kare", True),
    ("How do I turn on roaming?", "Enable roaming on my number", True),
    ("Roaming packs for UAE", "Roaming packs for USA", False),
    ("Price of the 299 plan", "Price of the 399 plan", False),
    ("How do I port my number to Tarang?", "Steps to port in to Tarang Mobile", True),
]

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")


def similarity(a: str, b: str) -> float:
    ea, eb = model.encode([a, b], normalize_embeddings=True)
    return float(ea @ eb)


scored = [(similarity(a, b), same) for a, b, same in PAIRS]
for th in (0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 0.98):
    hits = [same for sim, same in scored if sim >= th]
    false_hits = sum(1 for same in hits if not same)
    recall = sum(hits) / sum(same for _, same in scored)
    print(f"threshold {th:.2f}: recall {recall:.0%}, false hits {false_hits}")
semcache.note: classify_intent, llm_answer and current_tariff_version are stubs for your own intent classifier, model call and content version. RedisVL moved SemanticCache to redisvl.extensions.cache.llm in recent releases; older versions import it from redisvl.extensions.llmcache. The threshold script uses sentence-transformers; use the same embedding model as your cache.

code:
import litellm

PRICE_INR = {"claude-sonnet-5": (0.25 / 1000, 1.25 / 1000)}   # (input, output) per token, example

class BudgetExceeded(Exception):
    pass

class RunBudget:
    def __init__(self, run_id, max_inr=50.0):
        self.run_id, self.max_inr, self.spent = run_id, max_inr, 0.0

    def call(self, model, messages, **tags):
        if self.spent >= self.max_inr:
            raise BudgetExceeded(f"run {self.run_id} spent Rs {self.spent:.2f}")
        r = litellm.completion(model=model, messages=messages,
                               metadata={"tags": [f"{k}:{v}" for k, v in tags.items()] + [f"run:{self.run_id}"]})
        pin, pout = PRICE_INR[model]
        self.spent += r.usage.prompt_tokens * pin + r.usage.completion_tokens * pout
        return r

budget = RunBudget("recon-2026-09-27-0413")
reply = budget.call("claude-sonnet-5", [{"role": "user", "content": "Match these 40 UPI credits to invoices."}],
                    feature="reconciliation", customer="c-118")
print(round(budget.spent, 2))

routing.title: Blended cost of a cascade
routing.code:
def blended_cost(share_small, small_price, large_price, escalation_rate):
    # share_small of traffic starts on the small model; failures are re-asked on the large one
    small = share_small * small_price
    escalated = share_small * escalation_rate * small_price
    large = (1 - share_small) * large_price
    return small + escalated + large
routing.explain: An escalated request is re-asked on the large model, so it must be priced at large_price. Using small_price makes escalations look almost free and hides the real cost of a weak validator or a small model that fails often.

also.3: Correct: every request routed to the small model pays for the small call first, including the ones that later escalate.
also.5: Correct: traffic routed straight to the large model pays the large price once.

caching.title: Building a cached system prompt
caching.code:
def build_system(tools_doc, report, now):
    return [
        {"type": "text", "text": f"Current time: {now}"},
        {"type": "text", "text": tools_doc},
        {"type": "text", "text": report,
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
    ]
caching.explain: The current time is the first thing in the cached prefix, so the prefix changes on every call. Every request writes a new cache entry and none are ever read: caching then costs more than no caching. Variable content belongs after the breakpoint, in the user message.
caching.fix: # time removed here: send f"Current time: {now}" in the user message instead

also.4: Correct: tool documentation is stable and belongs in the cached prefix.
also.6: Correct: the breakpoint goes on the last stable block, so everything up to and including the report is cached.

controls.title: Compacting test output for a coding agent
controls.explain: The comment says the failures are at the end, but the code keeps the start of the log and throws the failures away. The agent then re-runs the tests to find them, which costs more steps than it saved. Keep the tail.

also.3: Correct: short logs are returned unchanged.

pruning.title: Summarizing old turns
pruning.code:
def prune(history, keep_recent=4, limit=16_000):
    # history[0] is the system prompt; it must always survive
    if tokens(history) <= limit:
        return history
    old, recent = history[:-keep_recent], history[-keep_recent:]
    summary = summarize(old)
    return [summary_message(summary)] + recent
pruning.explain: old starts at history[0], so the system prompt is summarized away with the chat. After the first prune the agent loses its instructions and tool rules. Split the system prompt off first and always send it.
pruning.fix:
system, old, recent = history[0], history[1:-keep_recent], history[-keep_recent:]
    summary = summarize(old)
    return [system, summary_message(summary)] + recent

also.3: Correct: nothing is pruned while the context is under the limit.
also.6: Summarizing the older turns is the right idea; the problem is what was put in old.
also.7: This line also omits the system prompt, but only because line 5 already put it into old. Fix the split and send history[0] first.

scheduling.title: Retrying rate-limited calls
scheduling.explain: 2 * attempt grows linearly (0, 2, 4, 6, 8 seconds) and the first retry is almost immediate. During an outage every client hammers the provider again at once. Exponential backoff doubles the wait each time: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 seconds, plus jitter.

also.3: Correct: a retry cap stops a permanent failure from retrying forever.
also.8: Correct: giving up after the cap lets the caller handle the failure.

batch.title: Reading batch results
batch.explain: Batch results can come back in any order, so pairing them with tickets by position saves answers against the wrong tickets. Match each result to its request by custom_id.

also.2: Correct: results are only available once processing has ended.
also.5: Correct: only succeeded results carry a message; the others should be collected for retry.

semcache.title: Setting the semantic cache threshold
semcache.code:
cache = SemanticCache(
    name="tarang_faq",
    redis_url="redis://localhost:6379",
    distance_threshold=0.90,          # we want similarity of at least 0.90
    ttl=24 * 3600,
    filterable_fields=[{"name": "scope", "type": "tag"}],
)
semcache.explain: RedisVL takes a cosine distance, not a similarity. Distance is 1 minus similarity, so 0.90 accepts any question with similarity as low as 0.10: almost every question matches something, and customers get confident answers to questions they never asked. A similarity of 0.90 is a distance of 0.10.

also.5: Correct: the TTL is in seconds, so entries live 24 hours.
also.6: Correct: a scope tag lets every lookup filter to shared answers only.

costattr.title: A per-run budget
costattr.code:
def call(messages, *, feature, customer, run):
    r = gw.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=messages, user=customer)
    run.add(r.usage)
    run.check_budget()
    return r
costattr.explain: The budget is checked only after the call, and the call has no feature or run tags. A run already over budget makes one more paid call, and the spend cannot be attributed.
costattr.fix:
run.check_budget()
    r = gw.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=messages, user=customer,
        extra_body={"metadata": {"tags": [f"feature:{feature}", f"customer:{customer}", f"run:{run.id}"]}})

also.3: Adding usage after each call is right.

2: Which router should you start with?
A trained classifier that predicts difficulty
Simple rules on intent or length
Rules are quick, explainable and need no training data. Train a router later, once you have outcome logs.
3: The small model answered. What happens before the answer is sent?
Nothing: the router already decided it was easy
A validator checks it: format, completeness, confidence
Routers make mistakes. A cheap check on every small-model answer catches most of them.
4: One small-model answer failed the check. What now?
Re-ask the same request on the large model
Return the small model’s answer with a warning
That is the cascade: escalate on failure, so a misroute costs latency rather than a wrong answer.
5: 8 small calls at 0.05 plus 3 large calls at 1, over 10 requests. What share of all-large spend?
(8 × 0.05 + 3 × 1) ÷ 10 = 3.4 ÷ 10 = 34%. The escalated request pays for both calls.
6: Spend fell. What must you watch next?
Quality per route, so savings don’t quietly cost accuracy
Nothing: the cost goal is met
A route whose pass rate drifts down is where customers get worse answers. Track it separately.

2: Where does the cache breakpoint go?
At the end of the stable content, before anything that varies
At the very end of the prompt, after the user’s question
Everything up to the breakpoint must be identical on every call. The question changes, so it goes after.
3: The first call writes 12,000 tokens to the cache. Is it cheaper than a normal call?
Yes, cached tokens are always cheaper
No, a write costs a little more, 1.25× on Anthropic’s 5-minute cache
The saving comes on later calls. The first one pays a small premium to store the prefix.
4: The second call arrives 2 minutes later with an identical prefix. What is billed at 0.1×?
The 12,000-token prefix
Only the new question
The prefix is read from cache at a tenth of the input price; the question is billed normally.
5: Someone moves the date into the system text above the breakpoint. What happens?
Nothing, dates are ignored by the cache
Every call misses, because the prefix changes every day
Caching matches the prefix exactly. One changed character before the breakpoint invalidates everything after it.
6: Over 20 calls, how many read the prefix from cache?
The first call writes; the other 19 read. That is why longer sessions save more.

2: The KYC task uses 3 of 14 tools. What should each call carry?
Only the 3 relevant tool definitions
All 14, so the model has every option
Every tool definition is paid for on every call. Load the ones the task needs.
3: Replies are about 900 tokens of prose. What is the lean fix?
Raise max_tokens so nothing is cut off
Cap max_tokens and ask for JSON fields
A cap plus a structured format shrinks output, which is also the most expensive token type.
4: The page reader returns 3,000 tokens of raw OCR text. What should the tool return?
The extracted fields the next step needs
The full text, in case it is useful later
Tool output stays in the context for every later step, so bulky output is paid for again and again.
5: The budget of 6 steps runs out mid-task. What should happen?
Keep going until the task is done
Stop gracefully and return a partial result for review
A budget that is ignored is not a budget. A graceful stop keeps the work useful and the cost bounded.
6: Tokens fell 79%. Are you done?
Yes, the cost goal is met
Only after the eval pass rate is confirmed
Caps and trimming can quietly remove information. Re-run the evals before calling it a win.

2: Context passes 16k tokens. When should you prune?
Before the next call
Only when the context window is full
Waiting for the window to fill means paying for a huge context on every turn until then.
3: Which turns should stay word for word?
The first 4, where the task was set
The most recent 4
The next reply depends most on recent turns. Older ones can be summarized.
4: What must the summary keep?
Decisions, client facts, figures and open tasks
Pleasantries and full tool outputs
A summary that drops a fact or an open task quietly breaks later answers.
5: A statement extract has been read and its figures recorded. What happens to the raw extract?
Keep it, it might be needed
Replace it with a short placeholder
Once its values are recorded, the raw output only costs tokens on every later turn.
6: Input paid fell from 441k to 190k tokens. What proves nothing important was lost?
Replaying long sessions and testing questions that need early facts
The lower token count itself
Savings are easy to measure; losses are not. Long-session evals catch dropped facts.

2: Why give interactive and background work separate queues?
So a bulk job never sits in front of a customer’s message
Because providers require it
With one queue, 200,000 summaries can block chat for hours.
3: The same note is enqueued twice. What should the second request do?
Run again to be safe
Skip: the work is already in flight or done
Deduplication removes work entirely, which is the cheapest saving there is.
4: The provider returns 429. When should you retry?
Immediately, and keep trying
After a growing delay with some randomness
Immediate retries during an outage multiply load and cost. Backoff with jitter spreads them out.
5: When should the nightly job run?
At 16:00, as soon as the data is ready
After midnight, when chat traffic is lowest
Off-peak work doesn’t add to the peak you have to reserve capacity for.
6: The background job now runs overnight. What happens to the capacity you need?
It drops to the interactive peak, 8 units
It stays at 11 units
Reserved capacity is sized to the busiest hour. Moving the job removes it from that hour.

2: What does every line of the batch file need, besides the request?
A unique custom_id
A timestamp
Results are matched back to requests by ID, so every request needs its own.
3: You submit the batch with a 24-hour window. When will results arrive?
Exactly 24 hours later
Any time within 24 hours, often much sooner
The window is the promise, not the schedule. Many batches complete within an hour.
4: How do you pair results with tickets?
By position in the output file
By custom_id
Results can come back in any order, so position is not reliable.
5: 3 of 100,000 requests failed. What do you resubmit?
The whole batch
Only the 3 failed IDs
Resubmitting everything pays for every request twice and wipes out the discount.
6: 100,000 tickets cost $750 in real time. What will the batch cost?
About $375
About $600
Major providers price batch requests at about 50% of standard rates.

2: “Roaming packs for UAE” and “Roaming packs for USA” score 0.91. With a 0.90 threshold, what happens?
The cached UAE answer is served for the USA question: a false hit
The cache sees the countries differ and misses
Embeddings measure overall meaning, and one word can change the answer. Tune the threshold on labelled near misses like this one.
3: Why are cached answers generated with user=None?
So a stored answer holds no personal details and is safe to share across the global scope
Because the model is cheaper without a user
Anything stored in a global scope may be served to any customer, so it must contain only shared facts.
4: A paraphrase arrives 30 hours after the entry was stored, with a 24-hour TTL. What happens?
A hit, because the meaning matches
A miss: the entry has expired, so the model answers and the entry is stored again
TTL bounds how old an answer can be. Past it, the entry is gone whatever the similarity.
5: The tariff page changes on Wednesday. With the version tag, what happens to Tuesday's price answers?
They keep being served until their 24-hour TTL runs out
They stop matching at once, because lookups filter on the new version
Tagging entries with the source version turns a content change into immediate invalidation; TTL alone would serve about 5,610 stale answers.
6: 45,600 hits a day at ₹0.40, and 60,000 lookups at ₹0.01. What is the daily saving?
Hits save ₹18,240 of LLM calls, but every FAQ question pays a ₹0.01 lookup: ₹18,240 − ₹600 = ₹17,640.

2: What does spend by tag reveal first?
Which features and customers the bill belongs to
The model’s accuracy
Attribution comes before optimisation.
3: A reconciliation run loops. What happens at ₹50?
It stops with a clear message
It runs all night
The run budget is checked before each call.
4: A free-tier account scripts thousands of requests. What stops it?
Its ₹500 daily key cap
Nothing
Caps per customer, not per account.
5: Spend on one tag triples overnight. What fires?
A spike alert
Nothing until month end
Anomaly detection by tag.
6: Monthly waste after the changes?
About ₹14,000
Loops ₹6,000 plus abuse ₹8,000.

routing: Send easy requests to a small, cheap model.
Keep the large model for requests that need it.
Rules or a trained router choose the model per request.
Try the small model first and escalate when a check fails.
A check on the cheap answer decides whether to escalate.
Track quality per route so savings don’t cost accuracy.
caching: The unchanging start of the prompt is stored and reused.
Put unchanging content first and the question last.
Cached input is billed at a fraction of the normal price.
Mark where the cached part ends, or rely on automatic caching.
Any change before the breakpoint causes a miss.
Entries expire after minutes; watch the hit rate.
controls: Cap output length per task type.
Limit how many steps or tool calls a task may take.
Load only the tools the task needs.
Return compact tool results, not full payloads.
Each step resends earlier context, so costs compound.
Check quality after tightening, and stop gracefully.
pruning: History piles up and is resent on every turn.
Every token in the context is paid for again on each call.
Older turns become a short summary.
keep recent turns or a window
Recent turns stay word for word.
Drop raw tool output once its values are recorded.
Pruning can drop facts, so test long sessions.
scheduling: Tag requests as interactive or background.
Send work through queues with separate worker pools.
Move non-urgent work to quiet hours.
Reserved capacity is sized to the peak, so lowering it saves money.
Limit usage per user or tenant.
Drop duplicates and retry with backoff.
batch: Many requests are submitted together as one asynchronous job.
Major providers charge about 50% of standard rates.
Results arrive within a window, often up to 24 hours.
Fits jobs nobody is waiting for.
Each request has an ID used to match results.
Track failures by ID and retry only those.
semcache: Questions are embedded and matched by meaning, not exact text.
the model is skipped on a hit
A hit returns the stored answer without calling the model.
a similarity threshold and false hits
The threshold trades hit rate against false hits.
Personal answers are never shared; account intents skip the cache.
Entries expire, and are purged when the source changes.
Unlike prompt caching, the model does not write a fresh answer.

routing: A broker’s assistant answers 50,000 questions a day. 85% are FAQs about brokerage charges and account opening, and every one runs on a frontier model. What is the biggest single saving?
Route FAQs to a small model and escalate failures
Raise max_tokens so answers are complete
Most traffic is easy, so moving it to a small model cuts the price of most tokens. Escalation protects the hard cases.
A small model costs 1/25 of the large one per request. You route 80% of traffic to it with no escalations. What share of the all-large spend remains?
Every request goes to a small model at $0.001 first; 15% fail validation and are re-asked on a large model at $0.02. What do 1,000 requests cost?
All 1,000 pay the small price ($1.00) and 150 escalations pay the large price ($3.00): $4.00, against $20.00 on the large model alone.
A claims assistant runs a cascade. Which signals are sensible triggers for escalating to the large model? Select all that apply.
The reply fails JSON schema validation
The model’s confidence field is below the threshold
A judge model scores the answer below the bar
The reply arrived in under one second
Escalation should depend on evidence that the answer is bad. Response speed says nothing about correctness.
After launching a router, cost fell 65%, but errors on plan-change requests rose fourfold. What should you do first?
Measure pass rate per route and per intent
Send everything back to the large model
Lower max_tokens on the small model
Per-route quality shows which intent is being misrouted, so you can fix that rule instead of giving up the savings.
A rebooking cascade tries a small model (0.5 s) on every request and escalates 30% to a large model (3 s). What is the average latency?
Every request pays 0.5 s, and 30% also pay 3 s: 0.5 + 0.3 × 3 = 1.4 s. Escalations pay for both calls.
You want to compare five small models on 500 labelled tickets this afternoon, behind one API key, before building a router. Which tool fits best?
OpenRouter gives hosted access to many models through one endpoint, which suits quick comparisons.
Which task is the strongest candidate for a small model?
Summarizing multi-specialty discharge notes for physicians
Drafting appeals for denied claims with legal reasoning
Explaining conflicting lab results to a patient
Short classification with a fixed label set is easy to validate and usually within a small model’s reach.
Before training a learned router for a contract-review assistant, what do you need? Select all that apply.
Outcome labels showing which model passed each request
A representative sample of real traffic
An eval that scores each model’s answers
A learned router is trained on real requests labelled with which model succeeded. A batch API is unrelated.
A router sends messages over 400 characters to the large model. The 60-character question “why was my UPI refund of INR 18,450 reversed twice?” goes to the small model and fails. What does this show?
The small model needs a larger max_tokens
Length is a weak proxy for difficulty; add intent rules or a validator
Short questions can be hard. Route on intent as well as length, and let a validator catch the misroutes.
200,000 grading requests a day cost $0.004 each on the large model. You route 90% to a small model at $0.0002, and 5% of those escalate. What is the new daily cost?
Which are genuine risks of a small-first cascade for shipment-status questions? Select all that apply.
Wrong answers when the validator misses a bad reply
Paying for two calls on every escalated request
Prompt caching stops working on the large model
Escalations are slower and cost two calls, and missed bad answers reach customers. Caching is unaffected.
An underwriting agent plans a task, then runs extraction and formatting steps. How should you split models?
Plan on the small model, format on the large one
Use the large model only for the final message
Plan on the large model; run extraction and formatting on a small one
Planning benefits from the strongest model; well-defined sub-steps such as extraction and formatting rarely need it.

For one request type the small model passes 90% and the large 98%; assume the large model gets right everything the small one does. The validator catches 80% of bad small-model answers. What is the cascade’s success rate?
Caught failures are fixed by the large model: 0.90 + 0.80 × (0.98 − 0.90) = 0.90 + 0.064 = 96.4%.
Two routing setups are proposed. Which metric compares them most fairly?
Cost per task at an equal success rate
Savings only count if quality holds, so compare cost per task at the same success rate.
You need provider fallbacks and per-team spend limits in a self-hosted proxy that every app calls. Which tool fits?
LiteLLM’s proxy offers one API across providers with fallbacks, budgets and spend tracking.
What should you log for every routed request to monitor a patient-FAQ router? Select all that apply.
Whether the validator passed or escalated
The patient’s full medical record in plain text
Route, validator outcome and cost let you track quality and savings per route. Logging full records adds privacy risk for no benefit.
A routing classifier costs 3% of a large-model call and sends 60% of traffic to a small model at 1/20 of the large price. What share of the all-large spend remains?
Classifier 0.03, plus small 0.6 × 0.05 = 0.03, plus large 0.4 × 1 = 0.4: 0.46 in total, so 46%.
Which properties make a request type a good candidate for the small model? Select all that apply.
The small model passes it at least 95% of the time on labelled traffic
Its answers can be validated cheaply
High volume, a proven pass rate and a cheap check are what make routing pay off safely.
Small-model answers must follow a fixed JSON schema, and 6% fail it. What is the best validator?
Ask the small model whether it is sure
Parse and validate against the schema; escalate on failure
A deterministic schema check is cheap and exact, and a failure is a clear signal to escalate.
Four steps score 97%, 97.5%, 94% and 96%. Errors compound. End to end?
Classification scores 97% on a small model and 98.5% on a large one, and the pipeline passes either way. What should you pick?
Small, since it meets the bar at a fraction of the cost
Pay only where a step needs it.
Why can a small model on an early step be a false saving? Select all that apply.
Its errors become inputs for later steps
Later steps usually cannot recover from them
A plan averages step accuracies to 96% and declares success. What is wrong?
Averages ignore compounding; the product is about 85%
It should use the minimum only
caching: A legal assistant sends a 30,000-token contract with each of 25 questions over 10 minutes, but the cache hit rate is 0%. The system prompt begins “Session started at 14:32:07”. What is the cause?
The contract is too long to cache
Caching only works with batch jobs
The timestamp at the top changes the prefix on every call
Any change before the breakpoint invalidates the cache. Move the timestamp after the stable content.
Base input is $3 per million tokens, cache writes cost 1.25× and reads 0.1×. A 16,000-token prefix is used on 8 calls within the cache lifetime. What does the prefix cost with caching?
One write: 16,000 × $3.75/M = $0.06. Seven reads: 112,000 × $0.30/M = $0.0336. Total $0.0936, against $0.384 uncached.
A 5,000-token catalogue prompt is reused on 40 calls within the cache lifetime. Writes cost 1.25× and reads 0.1× the base input price. What is the saving on the prefix?
Which changes will cause prompt-cache misses on a claims assistant? Select all that apply.
Putting each policyholder’s name at the start of the system prompt
Reordering the tool definitions between calls
Changing the question at the end of the prompt
Shuffling the few-shot examples on each call
Anything that changes the prefix breaks the cache. The final question sits after the breakpoint, so it is safe.
A support bot’s calls arrive about 30 minutes apart, and the provider’s default cache lifetime is 5 minutes. What happens?
Every call writes the cache again, so caching adds cost
The provider keeps the cache for a day
The entry expires between calls, so each call pays the write premium and nothing is read. A longer lifetime, where offered, fixes it.
A 12,000-token prefix uses a 1-hour cache (writes 2×, reads 0.1×). Calls arrive every 20 minutes for 3 hours: 10 calls. What is the saving on the prefix?
One write: 12,000 × 2 = 24,000 units. Nine reads: 9 × 1,200 = 10,800. Total 34,800 against 120,000: a 71.0% saving.
A semantic cache answers “What is the FD rate for 2 years?” with the stored answer for “What is the FD rate for 1 year?”. What went wrong?
The batch discount was applied twice
The router picked the wrong model
A near-duplicate match served a stored answer to a different question
Semantic caches reuse whole answers for similar questions, so a small but important difference can return a wrong answer.
You use Claude and want explicit control over what is cached, with an option for a 1-hour lifetime. What do you use?
Anthropic’s prompt caching uses cache_control breakpoints and offers 5-minute and 1-hour lifetimes.
What belongs in the cached prefix of an agent’s prompt? Select all that apply.
Stable content goes in the prefix. The user’s message changes every call, so it goes after the breakpoint.
A patient-FAQ bot on OpenAI has a 3,000-token system prompt. What do you need to do to benefit from prompt caching?
Send requests through the batch API
Nothing special: caching is automatic for long prompts, so keep the prefix stable
Nothing: OpenAI does not cache prompts
OpenAI caches long prompt prefixes automatically. Your job is to keep the start of the prompt identical.
A response’s usage shows 9,000 tokens read from cache, 1,000 uncached input tokens and no cache writes. What is the cache hit rate?
Hit rate = cached tokens ÷ all input tokens = 9,000 ÷ 10,000 = 90%.
Which workloads benefit most from prompt caching? Select all that apply.
A coding agent resending 40,000 tokens of repository context over 30 steps
Many users sharing one long instruction set
One-off prompts that are different every time
Chat over a fixed product manual
Caching pays when a long prefix repeats. Prompts that never repeat get nothing from it.
Prompt caching is turned on for a rebooking agent. Which costs does it NOT reduce? Select all that apply.
The new tokens in each user message
Input cost of the repeated prefix
Caching discounts only the repeated input prefix. Output, fresh input and request count are unchanged.
After adding a summary step that rewrites the history on every turn, a tutor bot’s cache hit rate fell from 85% to 20%. Why?
The cache has a daily quota
Rewriting history changes the prefix, so later content no longer matches
Caching needs an identical prefix. Prune less often, below the stable system prompt and tools.
Twelve lawyers will query the same 300-page case bundle all afternoon on Gemini. Which approach fits?
An explicit context cache with a lifetime that covers the afternoon
A semantic cache keyed by lawyer name
Explicit context caching suits very large context reused many times over a known period.
A merchant-support prompt has an 800-token stable prefix, and the model’s minimum cacheable prefix is 1,024 tokens. What saving does caching give?
0%: the prefix is below the minimum
Prefixes below the minimum are not cached at all, so there is nothing to save.
On the Claude API, where do you check whether caching is working?
cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens in the response usage
The model name in the response
The usage object reports tokens written to and read from the cache on every response.
A research assistant’s hit rate is 40%. Which changes could raise it? Select all that apply.
Move the analyst’s name and the date after the breakpoint
Keep tool definitions in a fixed order
Group questions about the same report close together in time
Put the question before the report
Stable, identically ordered prefixes and calls within the lifetime raise hits. Putting the question first breaks the prefix.
Base input is $3 per million tokens. A call reads a 10,000-token prefix from cache at 0.1× and adds 500 new input tokens. What is the input cost of the call?
What is the key difference between prompt caching and semantic response caching?
Semantic caching regenerates the answer each time
Prompt caching reuses the processed prefix but the model still generates a fresh answer
Prompt caching only discounts repeated input. A semantic cache returns a stored answer without calling the model.
controls: A KYC agent sometimes loops 15 times re-reading the same PDF pages. What is the most direct control?
A step budget with a graceful stop
A step budget caps the loop, and a graceful stop returns a useful partial result instead of failing.
A coding agent’s 8 steps use 2k, 4k, 6k … 16k tokens. You set a budget of 5 steps and trim tool output so each step is 40% smaller. Total tokens now?
The first five steps are 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30k; 40% smaller gives 30k × 0.6 = 18k, down from 72k.
Which changes reduce the tokens carried by each step of an agent? Select all that apply.
Returning only the needed fields from tools
Fewer tool definitions, compact results and short outputs all shrink a step. The budget limits the number of steps, not their size.
Measured replies for order-status questions have a 99th-percentile length of 320 tokens. How should you set max_tokens?
A little above 320, and handle truncated replies gracefully
Set the cap from measured lengths with a small margin, and handle the rare truncation.
Twenty tool definitions of 450 tokens each ride along on each of 12 calls in a task. Loading only 4 tools saves how many input tokens per task?
16 unneeded tools × 450 tokens × 12 calls = 86,400 tokens per task.
Removing examples from a clause-extraction prompt cut cost 20%, but accuracy fell from 95% to 88%. What is the lesson?
Re-run evals after trimming, and restore the examples that mattered
Prompt cuts can quietly lower quality. Evals show which cuts were free and which were not.
A triage agent loads tools dynamically, and 3% of requests get billing tools instead of scheduling tools. What should you add?
Load all 40 tools on every call
Remove tool descriptions to save tokens
Evals for the tool-selection step and a way to request more tools
Dynamic loading adds a selection step that can be wrong. Test it and give the agent a fallback.
Which are real cost drivers in agent loops? Select all that apply.
Tool outputs accumulate in the context
Tool definitions are resent on every step
Each extra step resends the whole history
Agents compound cost because every step resends a growing context. Output tokens are usually the most expensive kind.
Output costs $15 per million tokens. Replies shrink from 900 to 250 tokens on 10,000 replies a day. What is the daily saving?
A market-data tool returns 500 rows of ticks, but the agent only needs the latest price. What should the tool return?
A summary of the ticks from another LLM call every time
The latest price and timestamp, with a way to fetch more
Compact tool results keep every later step small; an option to fetch more covers rare needs.
You need a per-step breakdown of tokens and cost for every agent trace, self-hosted for data residency. Which tool fits?
Langfuse traces each step with token counts and cost and can be self-hosted.
You want to count tokens locally for OpenAI models before sending a prompt. What do you use?
tiktoken is OpenAI’s tokenizer library and counts tokens without a network call.
What should happen when an agent reaches its step budget? Select all that apply.
Return a partial result with what was done
Log the reason for later review
Flag the task for a person or a retry
A graceful stop keeps the work useful and visible. Ignoring the budget defeats it.
Normal runs take 5 steps; 20% of runs loop to 20 steps. Each step costs $0.02. What is the average cost per run with a budget of 8 steps?
Normal: 0.8 × 5 × $0.02 = $0.08. Looping, capped at 8: 0.2 × 8 × $0.02 = $0.032. Total $0.112, against $0.16 with no budget.
A tutor bot has max_tokens 150, and some answers stop mid-sentence. What is the fix?
Set the cap a little above the measured length of complete answers and handle max_tokens stops
Caps set below real answer lengths truncate work. Measure, add a margin and handle the stop reason.
A rebooking agent writes 400-token prose confirmations that a program then parses. What is the lean fix?
Ask for JSON with only the needed fields
Use a larger model for better prose
Structured output removes verbose prose and makes parsing reliable.
Which are signs that an agent is missing prompt and tool controls? Select all that apply.
The 99th-percentile steps per task are six times the median
Tool results over 5,000 tokens that are used once
Each task loads 30 tool definitions but uses 2
Long-tail loops, bulky one-use tool output and unused tool definitions are the classic waste. A high hit rate is good news.
A tenant’s key has a monthly spend limit of $500 and has spent $480. A runaway agent would spend $60 more. With a hard limit, how much more can it spend?
The limit stops spend at $500, so at most $20 more. It is a safety net under your own step budgets.
Which limits bound the cost of a single agent task? Select all that apply.
A per-key spend limit as a safety net
Steps, output per step and a spend ceiling each cap part of the cost. Temperature does not.
A claims task needs 5 steps, but the step budget is 3, and no task completes. What is wrong?
The budget is below what the task needs; set it from the steps successful runs take
Caps set too low stop tasks halfway. Base the budget on measured successful runs, with a margin.
pruning: Context starts at 3k tokens and grows by 3k a turn, so turns 1–6 send 3k, 6k, 9k, 12k, 15k and 18k. If pruning caps every turn at 9k, what is the total input?
Why does each turn of a long advisor chat cost more than the one before?
The whole history is resent and paid for on every turn
Models keep no state between calls, so every turn resends the growing context.
What should a running summary of a multi-day support ticket keep? Select all that apply.
Key figures such as amounts and dates
A summary must keep what later turns depend on. Pleasantries only cost tokens.
A sliding window keeps the last 6 turns. The plan the customer chose at turn 2 is forgotten by turn 12. What is the fix?
Summarize older turns, keeping key facts, instead of dropping them
Windows drop everything outside them. A summary keeps the facts while still shrinking the context.
A coding agent reads an 8,000-token test log once to find two failing tests. What should happen to the log?
Clear the raw log once the failing tests are recorded
Move it to the top of the prompt
Tool output that has been used only costs tokens on every later step. Record what matters, then clear it.
Each of 10 turns adds a 2,000-token tool output that is only needed on the turn it arrives. How many input tokens does clearing earlier outputs save across the session?
Without clearing, turn t carries (t − 1) old outputs: 2,000 × (0 + 1 + … + 9) = 2,000 × 45 = 90,000 tokens.
A contract Q&A pipeline puts the top 20 retrieved chunks in every prompt. Which changes cut retrieved context sensibly? Select all that apply.
Retrieve fewer chunks and re-rank them
Compress chunks with a tool such as LLMLingua
Fewer, better and de-duplicated chunks, or compressed ones, shrink input. Retrieving more does the opposite.
Pruning on every turn broke prompt caching for a tutor bot. Which design keeps both?
Put the summary before the system prompt
Keep the system prompt and tools above the pruned region and prune less often
Prune on every turn but smaller amounts
A stable top section keeps cache hits; infrequent pruning lets the rewritten history be reused for many turns.
A clinical assistant’s summary dropped a patient’s allergy. What is the best safeguard?
Pin critical facts outside the summarized region and test long sessions
Facts that must never be lost belong in a pinned section or external store, with evals that check them.
An agent must remember each policyholder’s preferences across sessions months apart. Which tool fits?
Mem0 stores memories outside the context and retrieves them when relevant.
You want to shrink long retrieved passages by removing low-information tokens before they reach the model. Which tool fits?
LLMLingua compresses prompts by dropping tokens that carry little information.
A summary call reads 14k tokens once and replaces them with a 1k summary. Each of the next 10 turns then sends 13k fewer tokens. Ignoring output, what is the net input saving?
10 × 13k = 130k saved, minus the 14k the summary call read: 116k.
Which symptoms show that context pruning is needed? Select all that apply.
Cost per turn rises steadily in long sessions
Sessions hit the context window limit
Old tool outputs and retrieved chunks dominate input tokens
Growing per-turn cost and bloated contexts are the signal. Two-turn sessions have little to prune.
Besides cost, why can a smaller context improve answers?
Models can miss information buried in the middle of long contexts
Studies such as “Lost in the middle” found models use information at the start and end of long contexts better than the middle.
Which parts of a shopping assistant’s context should normally survive pruning? Select all that apply.
Raw tool outputs that have already been used
Keep the instructions, the recent turns and pinned facts. Used tool output is the first thing to clear.
Context is 4k at turn 1 and grows by 2k a turn. You summarize when context is more than 12k. On which turn does the first summary happen?
Context at turn t is 2t + 2 thousand: turn 5 is exactly 12k, turn 6 is 14k, the first above the threshold.
A dispatch assistant needs shipment details from conversations up to three weeks old. What is the best approach?
Keep all three weeks in the context
Store facts externally and retrieve them by shipment ID
External memory keeps durable facts without carrying them in every prompt.
What are the costs or risks of summarization-based pruning? Select all that apply.
Summaries cost a call, can lose information and change the prefix. They do not change the window size.
In a quote-lookup assistant, only the last three turns ever matter. What is enough?
A sliding window over the recent turns
A knowledge graph of the whole conversation
When older turns are never needed, a simple window is the cheapest correct choice.
After pruning, a copilot sends a 2k system prompt, a 1k summary and the last 4 turns of 1.5k each. What is the context size?
scheduling: End-of-day report generation runs at 16:00 alongside live chat and sets the peak you reserve capacity for. What is the best move?
Move the reports to an off-peak queue overnight
Deferrable work moved to quiet hours stops adding to the peak.
Interactive load peaks at 10 units. A background job adds 4 units for 3 hours during that peak. If you move it to hours where interactive load is 2, what peak must you provision for?
The peak becomes max(10, 2 + 4) = 10 units, down from 14.
Which measures give fair use across tenants of a multi-tenant AI product? Select all that apply.
Separate queues for bulk and interactive work
One shared key with no limits
Limits, quotas and separate queues stop one tenant’s bulk job from starving the others.
Retries back off from 1 second and double each time, for up to 5 retries. What is the total wait if all 5 happen?
20% of catalogue-enrichment requests are duplicates created by retries and double submissions. What is the fix?
Run them on a larger model
Hash each request and skip ones already in flight or done
Deduplication removes work entirely, the cheapest saving there is.
A day’s work totals 120 unit-hours, and 10 units of capacity are reserved around the clock. What is the utilization?
During a provider incident, spend tripled because clients retried failed calls immediately and repeatedly. What is the fix?
Exponential backoff with jitter and a retry cap
Immediate retries create retry storms. Backoff spreads them out and a cap stops endless loops.
Which requests are good candidates for deferral to off-peak hours? Select all that apply.
Live chat with a customer whose SIM is blocked
Anything nobody is waiting on can be deferred. A blocked customer is waiting now.
You need Python task queues with separate worker pools, per-task rate limits and retries. Which tool fits?
Celery routes tasks to queues and supports rate limits, retries and scheduled runs.
A nightly job fans out 200,000 calls and must resume cleanly after a crash, with retries and timeouts. Which tool fits best?
Temporal runs durable workflows that survive crashes, with first-class retries and schedules.
Nightly enrichment calls can tolerate slow responses, but your code expects synchronous calls. Which OpenAI option lowers the price with a one-parameter change?
Flex processing trades slower, sometimes unavailable responses for a lower price, without switching to a batch workflow.
Patient chat and 50,000 discharge-summary jobs share one queue, and morning chat waits behind the jobs. What is the fix?
Separate queues and worker pools, with chat served first
Separate queues mean bulk work can never sit in front of a waiting patient.
Reserved capacity drops from 12 to 9 units at $3 per unit-hour. What is the saving over a 30-day month?
What are genuine downsides of request scheduling? Select all that apply.
Hard quotas can block legitimate spikes
Queue backlogs can hide failures without monitoring
It raises the price per token
