Scheduling trades delay and operational complexity for lower capacity costs. It does not change token prices.
On exam-results day, a hard per-school quota blocks students from the results assistant. What is the better policy?
Allow controlled bursts above the quota, with alerts
Quotas should protect against abuse without blocking legitimate spikes.
2,000 truck devices retry at exactly 1, 2 and 4 seconds after an outage and hit the API in synchronized waves. What is the fix?
Add random jitter to each delay
Jitter spreads clients out so they do not retry in lockstep.
Settlement summaries total 20 unit-hours of work. Data is ready at 01:00, and 4 units of spare capacity are available each hour from then. When does the job finish?
What does a priority queue in front of fixed reserved capacity do? Select all that apply.
Lets background work use spare capacity
Keeps the capacity you must reserve close to the interactive peak
Priorities protect users and fill idle capacity with deferred work. Token prices are unchanged.
Which requests belong on the interactive path? Select all that apply.
Anything a client is waiting for, or that is time-critical, stays interactive. End-of-day summaries can wait.
A Celery task has rate_limit="60/m", and 4 workers consume its queue. What is the most that can run per minute?
Celery task rate limits apply per worker instance, not globally: 4 × 60 = 240 a minute.
batch: A bank tags 200,000 support tickets every night for a dashboard read the next morning. What is the cheapest suitable approach?
The real-time API on a large model
Nobody waits on it, so a batch API at about half price is the natural fit.
20,000 requests each use 2,000 input and 300 output tokens, at $3 and $15 per million. What does the job cost as a batch at 50% off?
Which jobs are good fits for a batch API? Select all that apply.
Backfilling sentiment for last year’s reviews
Batch suits large independent jobs nobody is waiting on. A live question needs an immediate answer.
Batch results for 30,000 claim notes came back in a different order from the input file. How do you pair them with notes?
Results can arrive in any order, so each request carries a custom_id to match it back.
A 50,000-request batch finished with 2% failed. How many requests go into the follow-up batch?
2% of 50,000 = 1,000 failed IDs. Resubmit only those.

Each request has 1,000 shared input tokens read from cache at 0.1×, 500 unique input tokens and 100 output tokens. Prices are $3 and $15 per million, and the batch discount is 50%. What does one request cost?
A churn report is needed within one hour. Is a batch API a safe choice?
Yes: batches always finish within an hour
Yes, if the file is small
No: completion is only guaranteed within the batch window, often 24 hours
Only if you poll every minute
Many batches finish quickly, but only the window is promised. Tight deadlines need the real-time API.
Which make a workload a poor fit for a batch API? Select all that apply.
A user is waiting for the answer
Each result decides the next request
The deadline is shorter than the completion window
Batch needs independent requests and time to wait. Large independent jobs are exactly what it is for.
Two million support tickets already sit in a BigQuery table. Which batch option fits best?
Vertex AI batch prediction reads from and writes to BigQuery directly.
You run Claude and want up to 100,000 requests in one asynchronous job at half price. Which do you use?
The Message Batches API accepts up to 100,000 requests per batch at 50% of standard prices.
A job has 250,000 requests and the provider allows 100,000 per batch. How many batches do you submit?
What should you track for every request in a batch? Select all that apply.
Its status: succeeded, errored or expired
Its position in the input file
ID, status and destination make retries and audits reliable. Position is not reliable because order is not guaranteed.
Summarizing 12,000 contracts costs $0.02 each through the real-time API. How much does a batch at 50% off save?
12,000 × $0.02 = $240 standard; half of that, $120, is saved.
A nightly regression eval runs 8,000 test cases, and results are reviewed the next morning. What is the best way to run it?
Real-time, one case at a time
Eval suites are a textbook batch workload: independent requests and nobody waiting.
Some requests in a batch expired before processing. What should you do?
Move the whole pipeline to real-time for good
Resubmit only the expired IDs in a new batch
Track status per ID and retry only what did not complete.
Apart from price, what advantages do batch APIs offer? Select all that apply.
Separate, typically higher rate limits for batch work
No need to pace requests yourself
Tokens streamed as they are generated
The provider schedules the work within its own limits. Batch results are not streamed.
Through the real-time API, a job of 180,000 requests runs at a rate limit of 1,500 requests a minute. How long does it take?
A 60,000-request grading batch had 600 failures, and the team resubmitted the whole batch. What should they have done?
Resubmitting everything pays for 60,000 requests again to fix 600, wiping out the discount.
Which statements about batch APIs are true? Select all that apply.
Results can arrive in any order
On some providers the discount stacks with prompt caching
Completion is guaranteed within one hour
Batches return complete results in any order, and discounts can stack. Only the completion window, often 24 hours, is guaranteed.
A million eval requests cost $4,000 in real time. You move them to a batch at 50% off and to a model costing a quarter as much per request. What do they cost now?
semcache: A telecom support bot gets 1,00,000 questions a day, and thousands of them ask how to activate roaming in different words. Each pays for a fresh LLM answer. Which technique targets this directly?
Prompt caching of the system prompt
A semantic response cache keyed by question embeddings
Paraphrased repeats of the same FAQ can be served a stored answer when their embeddings are close enough, skipping the model entirely.
What is the key difference between prompt caching and a semantic response cache?
Prompt caching skips the model; a semantic cache does not
A semantic cache returns a stored answer without calling the model; prompt caching reuses the prefix but still generates a fresh answer
They are the same feature under different names
Prompt caching only works for images
Prompt caching cuts input cost while the model still answers; a semantic cache replaces the model call with a lookup.
A payments app caches answers globally. “Why was my UPI payment declined?” from one user returns another user’s answer. What is the root cause?
An account-specific intent was cached in a global scope
The embedding model is too small
Personal questions look alike across users but their answers differ. They must skip the cache or be scoped per user.
A cache hits 45,600 of the 60,000 FAQ questions it checks each day. An LLM answer costs ₹0.40 and a lookup ₹0.01. What is the net daily saving?
“Visa rules for UAE” and “Visa rules for USA” have similarity 0.91. The threshold is 0.90. What happens?
A false hit: the UAE answer is served for the USA question
The cache asks the user to clarify
Near misses score high because most words match. Tune the threshold on labelled near-miss pairs, or add a check on key entities.
RedisVL’s SemanticCache is configured with distance_threshold=0.08. What similarity does that require?
Cosine distance is 1 minus similarity, so a distance of at most 0.08 means similarity of at least 0.92.
Which questions are good candidates for a global semantic cache? Select all that apply.
How do I download my policy document?
What does a cashless claim mean?
What is the status of my claim?
Which documents are needed to file a motor claim?
How-to and policy explanations are shared. Claim status depends on the customer’s live record and must be generated fresh.

Tariffs change on Wednesday. Cached price answers have a 7-day TTL and are not purged. Tariff hits run at 13,500 a day. Using the rule of thumb that stale answers ≈ daily hits × TTL in days ÷ 2, roughly how many stale answers go out?
Entries written before the change expire gradually over 7 days, so on average half are stale: 13,500 × 7 ÷ 2 = 47,250.
With the same 13,500 tariff hits a day, the TTL is cut to 24 hours, still without a purge. How many stale answers now?
13,500 × 1 ÷ 2 = 6,750. A shorter TTL shrinks the stale window but does not close it; only a purge on change does.
A hospital chatbot caches “What are OPD timings?” globally. The timings change for the monsoon. What is the best fix?
Tag entries with the version of the timings page and purge or stop matching them when it changes
Invalidation tied to the source version retires old answers the moment the page changes, instead of waiting for expiry.
Which metrics should a team track for a semantic cache? Select all that apply.
False-hit rate from sampled human reviews
Number of tokens in the system prompt
Hit rate and savings show value; the false-hit rate shows the price paid in wrong answers. Prompt length belongs to prompt caching.
A B2B help desk serves many companies with different contracts. Which scope fits cached answers about “our SLA for P1 tickets”?
No cache at all is the only option
The answer depends on the company’s contract, not the individual user, so per-tenant scope shares it safely within one customer.
A per-user cache at 0.90 hits only 6% of questions. Why so low?
Individual users rarely repeat their own questions, so there is little to reuse
Per-user caches are not allowed to store answers
Embeddings do not work per user
Reuse comes from many people asking the same shared question. A per-user cache sees few repeats.
Lowering the threshold from 0.90 to 0.80 raises the hit rate from 46% to 60% on FAQ traffic, and the daily saving rises too. What should you check before shipping?
The false-hit rate on sampled hits, because many of the extra hits may be wrong answers
Saving counts false hits as money saved. Judge a threshold by false hits and saving together.
A wallet’s support bot adds a semantic cache. Which intents should skip it? Select all that apply.
How do I set a UPI PIN?
Refund status, balance and KYC outcome depend on the customer’s own records. Setting a UPI PIN is a shared how-to.
A cache stores answers generated with the student’s name and course inside them, then serves them globally. What is wrong?
Nothing, if the threshold is high
Personal details inside cached answers can be shown to other students
Only answers generated from shared facts, without personal details, belong in a shared scope.
1,00,000 questions a day. The cache is checked only for the 60,000 FAQ questions, with 48,000 hits. What is the hit rate over all traffic?
48,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = 48%. Against FAQ traffic alone it would be 80%, so say which base you use.
A team sets the threshold by trying a few questions by hand until results “look right”. What is the better approach?
Measure recall and false hits on a labelled set of paraphrase and near-miss pairs at several thresholds
Ask the LLM to pick a threshold
A labelled set turns the trade-off into numbers you can defend and re-check when traffic or the embedding model changes.
An NBFC’s FAQ cache must follow India’s DPDP Act principles. Which design choices help? Select all that apply.
Store only answers generated without personal data
Exclude loan-account intents from the cache
Set a TTL so entries do not live forever
Log full customer questions with PAN numbers in the cache key
Keeping personal data out of cached entries and limiting retention support data-minimisation. Storing PAN numbers in keys does the opposite. This is educational, not legal advice.
An LLM answer costs ₹0.50 and a lookup ₹0.02. At what hit rate on checked questions does the cache break even?
Every checked question pays ₹0.02; each hit saves ₹0.50. Break-even when hit rate × 0.50 = 0.02, so 4%.
costattr: What must every LLM call carry for cost attribution?
Tags such as feature, customer and run
Where is tagging easiest to enforce?
At one gateway or SDK wrapper
An agent run loops for hours. Best guard?
A per-run budget checked before each call
Stop the run, not the product.
Why is an account-wide hard cap risky?
It halts every customer when one run misbehaves
Which are useful cost tags? Select all that apply.
Waste of ₹1,20,000 + ₹80,000 falls to ₹6,000 + ₹8,000. Monthly saving?
Why budget in rupees rather than tokens?
A token on one model can cost 10× another.
Spend on a tag jumps to 3× its baseline. What should happen?
A budget check placed after the call means?
An over-budget run still makes one more paid call
Which tools support budgets or cost by tag? Select all that apply.
A customer key has a ₹500 daily cap. Most it can spend in a 30-day month?
Share of spend attributed rises from 0% to 98% of ₹8,00,000. Unattributed rupees remaining?
Calls made directly to the provider bypass the gateway. Effect?
Their spend is unattributed and unguarded
Which module-3 techniques lower the price per call?
This one makes spend visible and bounded.
What should a user see when a run hits its budget? Select all that apply.
How to continue or ask for help
Hard stops without run or customer tags stop 5,000 real runs a month. Fix?
Add run and customer tags so caps are specific
Which standard defines attributes for model, tokens and cost in traces?
Alerts at 80% of a ₹50 run budget fire at?

routing.q: Explain the difference between a router and a cascade, and when you would pick each.
pts: a cascade tries small first and escalates
routing.model: A router looks at the request and sends it to one model before anything runs, using rules or a trained classifier. A cascade sends every request to the small model first and escalates to the large one only when a validator or low confidence says the answer is not good enough. Pick a router when difficulty is predictable from the request and latency matters; pick a cascade when you have a reliable check on the answer, accepting extra latency on escalations.

routing.q: Your small model costs 1/20 of the large one. 80% of traffic can go to it, and 10% of those escalate. What share of the all-large spend remains? Show the working.
routing.model: Small calls: 0.8 × 0.05 = 0.04. Escalations: 10% of 80% is 0.08 of traffic, re-asked at full price, so 0.08. Direct large traffic: 0.2 × 1 = 0.2. Total 0.04 + 0.08 + 0.2 = 0.32, so 32% of the all-large spend remains.

routing.q: After launching a router, cost fell 70% but complaints rose. How do you find out what went wrong?
pts: check the validator or escalation rate
fix rules or retrain the router
routing.model: Break quality down by route and request type to find where answers got worse, usually hard requests misrouted to the small model. Check whether the validator is catching their bad answers and how often it escalates. Then tighten the routing rules for those intents, raise the confidence threshold, or retrain the router on the new outcome logs, and re-run the eval set before rolling out.

caching.q: Explain how prompt caching works and how you would structure a prompt to benefit from it.
pts: the provider stores the processed prefix
reads cost a fraction of input
caching.model: The provider stores the processed form of a prompt prefix and reuses it when the next request starts with exactly the same content. Cached reads bill at a fraction of the input price and are faster. So put everything stable first, tools, system prompt and reference documents, mark the breakpoint at its end (or rely on automatic caching), and put the user question, dates and IDs after it.

caching.q: The cache hit rate dropped from 90% to 0% after a release. What do you check?
pts: compare usage fields or diff prompts
caching.model: A drop to zero almost always means the prefix is no longer identical between calls. Diff the rendered prompts from two consecutive calls: look for a timestamp, request ID or user name added near the top, tool definitions or examples in a different order, or a changed system prompt. Confirm with the usage fields (cache reads versus writes), then move the variable content after the breakpoint.

caching.q: When can prompt caching cost you more than it saves?
caching.model: When writes are not followed by reads. On providers that charge extra for writes, a prefix that changes on every call, or calls spaced further apart than the cache lifetime, means every call pays the write premium and nothing is reused. Prompts below the minimum size are not cached at all. Caching pays when the same long prefix is reused several times within its lifetime.

controls.q: Why are agents so much more expensive than single LLM calls, and which controls address it?
controls.model: Each step resends the growing context, including every earlier tool result and all the tool definitions, so tokens compound with the number of steps, and a confused agent can loop. A step budget with a graceful stop caps the worst case; loading only relevant tools, trimming tool results to the fields needed and capping output shrink every step.

controls.q: How would you choose max_tokens and a step budget for a new task type?
pts: set a little above a high percentile
controls.model: Measure first: run the task on real traffic and record output lengths and steps per completed task. Set max_tokens a little above the 95th to 99th percentile of output length and the step budget a little above the steps successful runs need. Handle hitting either limit gracefully with a partial result, then re-run the evals to confirm the pass rate holds.

controls.q: A tool returns a 3,000-token record but the agent needs four fields. What do you change, and why does it matter more in agents?
pts: output stays in context for later steps
keep IDs to fetch more if needed
controls.model: Change the tool to return only the four fields, with an ID the agent can use to fetch more if it really needs it; paginate or summarize anything large. In an agent the tool result stays in the context and is paid for again on every later step, so a 3,000-token record over 10 steps costs 30,000 input tokens.

pruning.q: Explain why long conversations get more expensive every turn, and how pruning helps.
pts: models are stateless: history is resent
pruning.model: Models keep no memory between calls, so every turn resends the whole conversation and pays for it again; the cost of turn n grows with n. Pruning keeps the context small: recent turns stay verbatim, older ones become a summary of decisions and facts, and bulky tool outputs are cleared once used.

pruning.q: How do you prune without losing information the agent needs later?
pts: keep decisions, facts, figures and open tasks
pruning.model: Write the summary prompt to keep decisions, facts, figures and open tasks, and keep the most recent turns word for word. Record key values before clearing tool output, and store durable facts in external memory the agent can retrieve. Then replay long sessions with questions that depend on early facts to prove nothing important was lost.

pruning.q: How does context pruning interact with prompt caching?
pts: pruning rewrites history and breaks the cache
prune in larger, less frequent steps
keep system prompt and tools above the pruned region
pruning.model: Caching rewards a prefix that stays identical; pruning rewrites history, so everything after the change point misses the cache on the next call. Keep the system prompt and tools at the top, untouched, and prune in larger, less frequent steps so the rewritten history is itself reused for many turns before the next prune.

scheduling.q: Explain how request scheduling lowers LLM costs.
pts: lower peak means less reserved capacity
scheduling.model: Tag requests by urgency and send background work through its own queue. Moving that work to quiet hours lowers the peak, and reserved capacity only has to cover the peak, so you pay for less. Deduplication removes repeated work, per-tenant quotas stop one customer’s bulk job from driving spend, and backoff prevents retry storms.

scheduling.q: Chat peaks at 8 units. A nightly job adds 6 units from 16:00 to 20:00, when chat is 3 to 5 units. What capacity do you need now, and after moving the job to 00:00–08:00 at 3 units, where chat is 1 to 3?
scheduling.model: Before, the busiest hour is 16:00 with 5 units of chat plus 6 of the job: 11 units. After moving the job to 00:00–08:00 at 3 units, night load is at most 3 + 3 = 6, so the peak is the chat peak of 8. Capacity falls from 11 to 8 units, about 27% less.

scheduling.q: Why use exponential backoff with jitter for retries, and what goes wrong without it?
scheduling.model: When a provider is rate-limiting or down, immediate retries multiply load and cost exactly when capacity is scarce, and synchronized clients retry in waves. Exponential backoff doubles the wait each attempt, 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds, and jitter adds randomness so clients spread out. Cap the number of retries so permanent failures surface.

batch.q: Which workloads fit a batch API and which don’t? Give an example of each.
pts: does not fit: interactive or chained steps
batch.model: Batch fits work nobody is waiting on and where each request stands alone: nightly ticket tagging, eval suites, backfills, bulk summaries. It does not fit interactive chat, anything with a deadline shorter than the completion window (often 24 hours), or agent loops where each answer decides the next request.

batch.q: 10,000 requests, each 1,500 input and 200 output tokens, at $3 and $15 per million. What does the job cost standard and as a batch?
batch.model: Input: 10,000 × 1,500 = 15M tokens × $3 = $45. Output: 10,000 × 200 = 2M tokens × $15 = $30. Standard total $75; at 50% off the batch costs $37.50.

batch.q: How do you handle partial failures in a batch job?
pts: a unique custom ID per request
batch.model: Give every request a unique custom ID, and when results arrive record the status of each ID. Collect the errored and expired IDs and resubmit only those in a small follow-up batch, never the whole job. Make your writes idempotent, keyed by ID, so a retried item cannot create duplicates.

semcache.q: Explain how a semantic response cache works and how it differs from prompt caching.
pts: stored answer returned, no model call
prompt caching still generates a fresh answer
semcache.model: Each question is embedded and compared with cached questions. If the nearest one is above the similarity threshold, in the same scope and not expired, its stored answer is returned and the model is not called. Prompt caching is different: the provider reuses the processed prompt prefix, but the model still writes a fresh answer. A semantic cache saves more per hit, but risks false hits on near-miss questions, stale answers after content changes, and leaks if personal answers are shared.

semcache.q: At a 0.90 threshold, 60,000 FAQ questions a day go through the cache and 45,600 hit. An LLM answer costs ₹0.40 and a lookup ₹0.01. What is the daily saving, and why is a 0.80 threshold with a higher saving not better?
semcache.model: Hits avoid 45,600 × ₹0.40 = ₹18,240; lookups cost 60,000 × ₹0.01 = ₹600; net ₹17,640 a day. A 0.80 threshold hits more often, but many of the extra hits are false: near-miss questions get another question’s answer. Saving counts a false hit as money saved, so it must be read next to the sampled false-hit rate.

semcache.q: After launching a semantic cache, a customer sees another customer’s bill amount, and prices stay wrong for days after a tariff change. Diagnose both and fix them.
pts: account answers in a shared cache
exclude those intents or scope per user
purge or version on source change
semcache.model: “What is my bill?” looks the same for every customer, so in a global cache one customer’s answer matched another’s question. Account-specific intents must skip the cache, and anything stored must be generated without personal data and tagged with its scope. The wrong prices came from long-lived entries written before the change. Tag entries with the source version and stop matching or purge them when the tariff page changes, rather than waiting for the TTL.

costattr.q: How would you control LLM spend in a multi-tenant agent product?
costattr.model: Route every call through a gateway that requires team, feature, customer and run tags; report spend and unit cost by tag; add per-run budgets and per-customer caps; alert at 80% and flag spikes by tag.

costattr.q: After a ₹1,20,000 surprise, someone proposes a hard cap on the whole account. Your view?
costattr.model: An account-wide cap would halt all customers when one run loops. Tag calls first, then cap each run and each customer, keep alerts on the account total, and investigate spikes by tag.

cases.tag: Paying twice for the same prompt
cases.title: The claims agent that tripled the bill
cases.brief: An insurer replaced its claims FAQ bot with an agent that checks claim status, classifies uploaded documents and drafts replies. Quality went up and nobody wants to lose that. The monthly bill went from ₹6 lakh to ₹19 lakh, and finance wants it under ₹8 lakh within a quarter. Conversations are short - a median of four turns - and the insurer pays per token with no reserved capacity.
evidence: 92% of calls go to the frontier model, yet 70% of requests are status checks and document-type classification that a small model passes 96% of the time in offline tests.
Every step resends a 9,000-token system prompt with 22 tool definitions. The provider dashboard shows a 0% cache hit rate - the prompt begins with the current time and the claim ID.
The median task takes 6 steps, but 8% of tasks run past 25 steps and account for 35% of spend. Tool calls return full claim records of about 4,000 tokens each.
A nightly job re-summarises 40,000 open claims through the real-time API at 22:00. Nobody reads the summaries before 09:00.
Finance cannot say which feature or which customer the ₹19 lakh belongs to, and there is no cap on a single run.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.caching: Start here, because it is the largest saving available for the least risk and the least work. A 9,000-token prompt with 22 tool definitions is resent every step at a 0% hit rate, and the reason is one line: the prompt opens with the current time and the claim ID. Move the volatile parts to the end, keep the stable prefix byte-identical, and the cache starts working - with no change to behaviour and nothing to re-evaluate.
why.routing: 70% of requests are status checks and classification that a small model passes 96% of the time, and 92% of calls go to the frontier model anyway. Route by step rather than by request, measure quality per route rather than end to end so a weak step cannot hide, and keep the hard drafting work on the big model - that is where the quality gain finance does not want to lose actually lives.
why.controls: 8% of tasks run past 25 steps and consume 35% of spend, and every tool call returns a 4,000-token claim record. Cap steps, trim tool payloads to the fields the agent uses, and deduplicate the prompt that has grown over time. Watch the pitfall: caps set too low stop tasks halfway, so set them from the distribution rather than by feel.
why.batch: Useful and nearly free: 40,000 nightly summaries that nobody reads until 09:00 are running through the real-time API at full price for no reason. Move them to the batch API, track partial failures by ID, and split the job so it does not hit size limits.
why.costattr: Useful, and the reason this got to ₹19 lakh before anyone noticed: nobody can attribute spend to a feature or a customer, and a single run has no cap. Tag by feature, customer and run, and set per-run and per-tenant guards rather than one account-wide cap that would take the whole product down.
why.pruning: Not needed: conversations have a median of four turns, so there is no long accumulated context to prune. Note also that pruning changes the prompt prefix, which would fight the cache fix that is your biggest win here.
why.scheduling: Not needed: the insurer pays per token with no reserved capacity, so there is no hourly commitment to fill and no fair-use problem described. The deferrable work is handled better by the batch API.
why.semcache: Not needed: these answers are about one claimant's specific claim, and a shared response cache serving one customer's claim details to another is the documented failure mode. The FAQ bot it replaced might have wanted this; the agent does not.

firstWhy.routing: The biggest structural saving and your second step - 92% of calls on the frontier model for work a small model passes is the headline waste. But it is also the one change that can cost quality, so it needs per-route evaluation and a careful rollout, while the cache fix is a reordering of the prompt with no behavioural risk at all. Take the free money first.
firstWhy.controls: Right about where the tail spend is: 8% of tasks taking 35% of spend is a striking number. But a step cap set before you have moved cheap steps to a small model is a cap chosen against the wrong cost curve, and trimming tool payloads changes the prompt - which matters once the cache is working.
firstWhy.batch: Correct, easy and genuinely free, and you should do it this week alongside the cache fix. As the headline first move, though, the nightly job is one job - the recurring waste is 9,000 tokens resent on every step of every task all day.

cases.model: Start with prompt caching, because a 9,000-token prefix with 22 tool definitions is being resent on every step at a 0% hit rate, and the cause is that the prompt opens with the current time and the claim ID - move the volatile values to the end, keep the prefix byte-identical, and a large share of the bill disappears with no behavioural change and nothing to re-evaluate. Then route by step: 70% of requests are status checks and classification a small model passes 96% of the time, so move those while keeping drafting on the frontier model, and measure quality per route rather than end to end so a weak step cannot hide. Next add prompt and tool controls - cap steps using the real distribution rather than a guess, since 8% of tasks past 25 steps take 35% of spend, and trim 4,000-token claim records down to the fields actually used. Move the 40,000 nightly summaries nobody reads before 09:00 to the batch API, tracking partial failures by ID. Finally tag spend by feature, customer and run and set per-run guards rather than one account-wide cap. Context pruning has nothing to prune at four turns and would disturb the cache prefix; there is no reserved capacity to schedule against; and a shared semantic cache over claim-specific answers would serve one customer's details to another.
cases.note: The first move here was not the biggest number but the cheapest reversible one: a prompt reordering with no quality risk, before a model change that needs evaluating. Case 2's traffic is nothing but repeated questions, and Case 3's sessions run for hours - both move the answer somewhere else entirely.

caching: Symptom 2 contains its own answer if you read it twice: 9,000 tokens of system prompt and tool definitions resent every single step, a 0% cache hit rate, and a prompt that begins with the current time and the claim ID. Why is the hit rate zero?
The saving comes from a prefix that does not change between calls. Something at the very front of this prompt changes on every call, and it is invalidating everything behind it.
Prompt Caching. The first pitfall - one changed character early in the prompt invalidating everything after it - is this symptom exactly.
routing: Symptom 1: 92% of calls go to the frontier model, and 70% of requests are status checks and document classification that a small model passes 96% of the time. What is the mismatch?
Not every step of a task needs the same model. The question is how you decide per step - and how you measure so that a weak step does not hide inside a good end-to-end number.
Model Routing and Tiering. Read the pitfall about measuring only end to end, and the one about cascades adding latency.
controls: Symptom 3 has two halves: 8% of tasks run past 25 steps and account for 35% of spend, and every tool call returns about 4,000 tokens of full claim record. What is being consumed that nobody asked for?
Steps and payload. Limit how far a task may run, and return the fields that get used rather than the whole record - but be careful how low you set any limit.
Prompt & Tool Controls. Note the pitfall about caps set too low truncating answers or stopping tasks halfway.

drop.pruning: Context pruning helps long conversations and multi-hour sessions. What is the median number of turns here - and what does pruning do to a prompt prefix you are trying to cache?
drop.scheduling: Request scheduling earns its keep against reserved capacity you pay for by the hour, or multi-tenant fair use. What does the brief say about how this insurer pays?
drop.semcache: Semantic response caching serves a stored answer to the same question asked differently. These answers are about one claimant's own claim - what is the documented failure mode of a shared cache there?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Now sort by risk as well as size: one of these is a reordering of text that changes no behaviour and needs no re-evaluation, and another swaps the model that answers your customers.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: 92% of calls use the frontier model for work a small model handles, which is the largest structural waste in the system.
A volatile value at the front of the prompt makes a 9,000-token prefix uncacheable on every step - a large saving with no behavioural risk.
8% of tasks consume 35% of spend, so the long tail is where the concentrated money is.
whyFirst.why: Order by saving per unit of risk when a quality gain is explicitly not to be lost. Routing is the bigger structural win and it is your second step, but it changes which model answers customers and needs per-route evaluation. Moving a timestamp to the end of a prompt changes nothing anyone can observe except the bill - and it pays on every step of every task, all day.

cases.tag: The same question, four lakh times
cases.title: The bot that answers the same forty questions all month
cases.brief: A telecom operator runs a support bot across nine prepaid brands. Turns are short, everything is interactive, nothing can wait, and there is no reserved capacity. Finance bills each brand a flat internal fee and has started asking whether that is remotely fair. An earlier attempt to cut the bill was switched off after it answered the wrong question confidently.
evidence: 61% of monthly volume is forty distinct questions asked in different words - tariffs, roaming rates, how to port. Every one of them is a full model call.

A semantic cache was tried once: the threshold was loose enough that “roaming in UAE” was served the answer for “roaming in USA”, and the cache was global, so one customer saw another's account balance. It was switched off rather than tuned.
The system prompt and fourteen tool definitions - about 7,000 tokens - are resent on every turn, and the prompt opens with a per-session greeting containing the customer's name.
Spend per brand is unknown. Some calls go directly to the provider and skip the gateway and its tags entirely.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.semcache: Start here, because 61% of volume is forty questions in different clothes, and a lookup is both cheaper and faster than a model call. The previous attempt failed for two specific, fixable reasons rather than because the idea is wrong: the threshold was too loose, so “UAE” matched “USA” - the textbook example - and the cache was global, so account answers leaked between customers. Cache only answers that depend on shared content such as tariffs and how-to steps, never anything account-specific, tune the threshold on labelled pairs, and set a TTL short enough that a tariff change is not served for weeks.
why.caching: 7,000 tokens of prompt and tool definitions resent every turn at no hit rate, because the prompt opens with the customer's name. Move the greeting to the end, keep the prefix identical across sessions, and every call that does miss the response cache gets much cheaper. It is the companion fix to the first and carries no behavioural risk.
why.costattr: Nine brands billed a flat fee with no idea what each costs, and calls bypassing the gateway so they are not even counted - that is the named pitfall and it means any saving you report is unverifiable. Route everything through the gateway, tag by brand and feature, and set per-brand guards rather than one account-wide cap.
why.routing: Useful: the forty FAQ answers that do miss the cache are easy work a small model handles, and so is intent classification. Secondary because a cache hit costs less than any model, however small.
why.controls: Useful: fourteen tool definitions on a bot whose traffic is 61% FAQ suggests the prompt has accumulated, and trimming it compounds with the caching fix. Modest savings next to the first two.
why.pruning: Not needed: turns are short and there is no long accumulated context. Pruning would also disturb the prompt prefix you are trying to make cacheable.
why.scheduling: Not needed: there is no reserved capacity to fill and nothing deferrable - every request has a customer waiting on it.
why.batch: Not needed: batch processing trades latency for price, and this workload has no latency to trade. The nightly-job answer from Case 1 has no equivalent here.

firstWhy.caching: Right, risk-free and your second step - a per-session greeting at the front of 7,000 tokens is the same mistake Case 1 made with a timestamp. But prompt caching makes each model call cheaper, while 61% of calls should not be model calls at all. Remove the call before optimising it.
firstWhy.costattr: The most important thing for finance and genuinely essential - with calls skipping the gateway you cannot even measure what you are about to save. Instrument now, in parallel. As the first move, though, it changes no spend by itself; it tells you where the spend is, and here the evidence already does.
firstWhy.routing: Reasonable: forty FAQ answers do not need a frontier model. But a small model answering the same question four lakh times is still four lakh calls, and the cheapest possible model call costs more than a lookup.

cases.model: Start with semantic response caching, because 61% of monthly volume is forty questions rephrased and a lookup beats any model call on both cost and latency. Fix the two reasons the earlier attempt failed rather than accepting its verdict: tune the similarity threshold on labelled pairs so “roaming in UAE” cannot match “roaming in USA”, and scope the cache so it holds only answers that depend on shared content - tariffs, roaming rates, porting steps - and never account-specific ones, which is how one customer saw another's balance. Set a TTL short enough that a tariff change is not served for weeks. Then fix prompt caching: 7,000 tokens of prompt and tools are resent every turn because the prefix opens with the customer's name, so move the greeting to the end and keep the prefix identical across sessions. Next close the attribution gap - stop calls bypassing the gateway, tag by brand and feature, and set per-brand guards rather than one account-wide cap - because nine brands on a flat internal fee cannot be priced or policed otherwise. Route the remaining FAQ misses and intent classification to a small model, and trim the fourteen tool definitions. Pruning, scheduling and batch all address workload shapes this bot does not have.
cases.note: A failed experiment is not a verdict on the technique: the semantic cache was switched off for a loose threshold and a global scope, both of which are named pitfalls with named fixes. Read why something failed before crossing it off.

semcache: Symptom 1: 61% of monthly volume is forty distinct questions asked in different words, and each one is a full model call. What is the cheapest possible way to answer a question you have already answered?
Not a smaller model - no model at all. Look it up. The hard parts are deciding when two questions are really the same, and which answers are safe to share.
Semantic Response Caching. Its three pitfalls are symptom 2 almost word for word: a loose threshold matching UAE to USA, a global cache leaking account answers, and a long TTL serving old prices.
caching: Symptom 3: about 7,000 tokens of prompt and tool definitions on every turn, and the prompt opens with a per-session greeting containing the customer's name. What does that do to the part of the prompt that never changes?
A saving that depends on the beginning of the prompt being identical call after call. Something personal has been placed right at the front.
Prompt Caching. Read the pitfall about one changed character early in the prompt - and notice this is the same mistake as Case 1 in different clothing.
costattr: Symptom 4: nine brands billed a flat internal fee, no idea what each actually costs, and some calls going straight to the provider and skipping the gateway. What can you not do - including about the savings you are planning?
You cannot attribute spend, so you cannot price fairly, cap per brand, or prove that any of your other fixes worked. One detail in this symptom makes even the measurement incomplete.
Cost Attribution and Budget Guards. The first pitfall - calls that skip the gateway and its tags - is symptom 4, and the second warns against the obvious over-correction.

drop.pruning: Context pruning helps long sessions whose context has accumulated. What does the brief say about turn length here - and what would pruning do to a cacheable prefix?
drop.scheduling: Request scheduling fills reserved capacity and separates deferrable work from interactive paths. What does this bot have that is deferrable, and what capacity is being paid for by the hour?
drop.batch: Batch processing trades hours of latency for about half the price. Who is waiting on each of these requests?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right, and two of them attack the same bill from opposite ends. Ask which one removes calls altogether rather than making each call cheaper - and read why the earlier attempt was abandoned before deciding it cannot be done.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: 61% of volume is forty repeated questions, and a lookup is cheaper and faster than the cheapest model call.
A per-session greeting at the front of a 7,000-token prompt makes the whole prefix uncacheable on every turn.
Calls bypass the gateway, so nothing is attributable and no saving can be verified.
whyFirst.why: Order by whether you are making a call cheaper or removing it. Prompt caching is risk-free and must happen, and attribution has to be instrumented in parallel or you cannot prove any of this worked - but both leave 61% of volume as model calls. Serving a cached answer to a repeated FAQ removes the call, which beats any price you could negotiate for making it.

cases.title: The research agent that runs for nine hours
cases.brief: An asset manager runs a research agent over company filings: it reads annual reports and transcripts, builds comparisons and drafts analyst notes. Sessions are long, the work is genuinely hard throughout, and the firm pays for reserved capacity by the hour alongside its per-token spend. One run last month cost more than an analyst's monthly salary, and the fix someone applied made the agent forget a number it needed.
evidence: Sessions run four to nine hours and read whole filings. By hour three the context holds about 400,000 tokens of pages already summarised, and every later call pays for all of it.
A pruning attempt summarised aggressively, dropped a figure the agent needed at hour six, and also rewrote the prompt prefix - cancelling the prompt-cache savings the firm already had.

70% of the work is ingesting and tagging 12,000 filings that nobody waits on. It runs through the real-time API during market hours, competing with interactive analyst chat for the reserved capacity the firm pays for hourly.
One run looped for eleven hours and cost ₹2.4 lakh. There is a single account-wide hard cap, and when it tripped the entire product went down for every analyst.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.pruning: Start here, because it is the only item that changes the shape of the cost rather than its price. By hour three the agent carries 400,000 tokens of pages it has already summarised, and every subsequent call pays for all of them - in a nine-hour session that is most of the bill. Prune carefully: keep what later steps will reference, retain figures verbatim rather than in prose summaries, and - the lesson of the failed attempt - prune from the end so the cached prefix survives.
why.batch: 70% of the work is ingesting and tagging 12,000 filings that nobody is waiting on, and it is running through the real-time API. Move it to the batch API for roughly half the price, track partial failures by filing ID, and split the job so it does not hit size and rate limits. This is the largest saving on the page that costs nothing in quality.
why.costattr: An eleven-hour run costing ₹2.4 lakh with no per-run cap is one failure; a single account-wide cap that took the whole product down for every analyst when it tripped is the other, and it is a named pitfall. Set per-run and per-analyst guards, tag spend by run and by desk, and set budgets in money rather than tokens since prices differ several-fold between models.
why.scheduling: Useful and the other half of symptom 3: once the ingestion is batched, schedule it off market hours so it stops competing with interactive analyst chat for reserved capacity, and keep the interactive path on its own lane. Allow controlled bursts rather than hard quotas so a legitimate spike is not blocked.
why.controls: Useful: an eleven-hour loop suggests no step cap at all, and filings returned whole are large payloads worth trimming to the sections used. Set the cap from the real distribution, because a genuine nine-hour session must not be cut off at hour four.
why.caching: Useful, and mostly a matter of not breaking it: the firm already had prompt-cache savings and the pruning attempt destroyed them by rewriting the prefix. Keep the stable instructions and tool definitions at the front, and change only the tail.
why.routing: Not needed on this evidence: the work is hard throughout and no measured slice is easy. Reading a filing and building a comparison is not a status check - and nobody has shown a step a small model passes.
why.semcache: Not needed: each question concerns a specific filing at a specific moment, and a response cache would serve last quarter's analysis as this quarter's - the TTL pitfall with real money behind it.

firstWhy.batch: The largest single saving here, free in quality terms, and you should start it this week - 70% of the work at roughly half price is hard to argue with. As the first move, though, it fixes the part of the workload nobody watches, while the interactive sessions analysts actually use keep paying for 400,000 tokens of already-summarised pages on every call.
firstWhy.costattr: Urgent for a different reason than cost: a single account-wide cap that takes the product down for everyone is an availability bug, and it should be split immediately. But guards bound the damage of a long session rather than making long sessions cheaper, and the 400,000-token context is why they are expensive in the first place.
firstWhy.scheduling: Correct that ingestion should not compete with analysts for reserved capacity during market hours. But scheduling decides when work runs, and most of this work should not be running on the real-time API at all - decide that first, and scheduling becomes a detail of it.

cases.model: Start with context pruning, because it is the only change that alters the shape of the cost: by hour three the agent carries about 400,000 tokens of pages it has already summarised, and every later call in a nine-hour session pays for all of them. Prune with the failed attempt in mind - keep figures verbatim rather than paraphrased so hour six still has what it needs, keep what later steps reference, and prune from the tail so the cached prefix survives, since rewriting the prefix is what cancelled the savings the firm already had. Then move the 70% of work that nobody waits on - ingesting and tagging 12,000 filings - to the batch API at roughly half the price, tracking partial failures by filing ID and splitting the job to stay inside size limits. Next fix the budget guards: replace the single account-wide cap, which took the whole product down for every analyst when it tripped, with per-run and per-analyst limits set in money rather than tokens, and tag spend by run and desk. Schedule the batched ingestion outside market hours so it stops competing for reserved capacity, keeping the interactive lane separate and allowing controlled bursts. Add a step cap drawn from the real distribution, and keep stable instructions at the front of the prompt so caching keeps working. Routing has no easy slice to exploit here, and a response cache would serve stale analysis.
cases.note: Three cases, three different first moves - a prompt reordering, a lookup, and a context strategy - and in each one the technique that dominated elsewhere was irrelevant. The question was never which technique saves most in general, but which one matches the shape of the workload: short turns, repeated questions, or long sessions.

pruning: Symptom 1: by hour three the context holds about 400,000 tokens of pages the agent has already summarised, and every later call pays for all of it. In a nine-hour session, what does that do to the bill?
The window is carrying material whose value has already been extracted. Removing it is the fix - and symptom 2 is a catalogue of how to do it badly.
Context Pruning. All three pitfalls are in symptom 2: summaries dropping details needed later, broken references to earlier turns, and a changed prefix cancelling prompt-cache savings.
batch: Symptom 3: 70% of the work is ingesting and tagging 12,000 filings that nobody waits on, running through the real-time API. What is being paid for that nothing requires?
Immediacy. There is an API tier that gives up streaming and real-time answers in exchange for roughly half the price, which suits a job whose results nobody is watching.
Batch Processing. Note the pitfalls about tracking partial failures by ID and splitting very large jobs.
costattr: Symptom 4 has two failures in one sentence: an eleven-hour run costing ₹2.4 lakh with nothing stopping it, and a single account-wide cap that took the product down for every analyst when it finally tripped. What is wrong with each?
One run needs its own ceiling; the account does not need one ceiling for everybody. And you need to know whose spend is whose - note what units a budget should be set in.
Cost Attribution and Budget Guards. Read the pitfall about a single account-wide hard cap, and the one about budgets set in tokens while prices differ between models.

drop.routing: Model routing moves easy steps to a smaller model, and it needs a measured easy slice. What does the brief say about the difficulty of this work, and which step has anyone shown a small model passes?
drop.semcache: Semantic response caching serves a stored answer to a rephrased question. These answers concern a specific filing at a specific time - what does the TTL pitfall imply about caching them?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right. Now separate making the work cheaper from bounding it: two of these put a price or a limit on the work, and one changes how much the work costs per call for every hour it runs.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A single account-wide cap already took the whole product down for every analyst, which is an availability failure as well as a cost one.
70% of the work needs no immediacy at all and is running at full real-time price, which is the largest clean saving available.
Every call after hour three pays for 400,000 tokens of already-summarised pages, which is what makes a nine-hour session expensive at all.
whyFirst.why: Order by what drives the cost rather than what caps or reprices it. Batching is the biggest clean win and should start immediately; splitting that account-wide cap is urgent for availability regardless. But both leave the interactive sessions analysts use all day paying for a context that grows with every page read - and that compounding is the reason a single run could reach ₹2.4 lakh in the first place.

quiz: 90% of your 40,000 daily requests are simple FAQs, and all of them run on a frontier model. What's the biggest single saving?
Most traffic is easy, so sending it to a small model cuts the price of the bulk of your tokens.
Your 10k-token system prompt is the same on every call, but the prompt-cache hit rate is 0%. What's the most likely cause?
The prompt is too short to cache
A timestamp or request ID near the start of the prompt
Anything that changes before the cache breakpoint invalidates the cache. Move variable content to the end.
Why does each turn of a long chat cost more than the one before?
The whole history is resent and paid for on every turn
Models are stateless: every turn resends the growing context, so input tokens compound.
A nightly job tags 200,000 support tickets. What's the cheapest fit?
Real-time API with a large model
Nobody waits on it, so a batch API at about half price is the natural fit.
After adding context pruning, costs fell less than expected and the prompt-cache hit rate dropped. Why?
Pruning changed the prompt prefix, so cached tokens no longer matched
Pruning rewrites history, which changes the prefix after that point and cancels cache savings. Prune in larger, less frequent steps below the stable prefix.
Base input costs $3 per million tokens and cache reads cost 0.1×. An 8,000-token cached prefix is read 100 times. What do those reads cost?
Some tasks make your agent loop 15 steps. What's the most direct control?
A step budget with a graceful stop
A step budget caps the loop; a graceful stop returns a useful partial result instead of failing.
A small model costs 1/10 of the large one. You route 70% of traffic to it. New spend compared with all-large?
Peak traffic at 11 am forces reserved capacity sized for the peak, and background summaries also run then. Best move?
Move background work to an off-peak queue
Shifting deferrable work lowers the peak you must provision for, without touching interactive users.
Which technique lowers the price per token without changing the model?
Batch APIs bill the same model at a discount. Pruning, budgets and deduplication reduce the number of tokens or requests instead.

routing.t: Large model: $10 per 1,000 requests. Small: $0.50. You route 75% to the small model, and 10% of those escalate to the large one. Cost per 1,000 requests, in $?
routing.a: Small: 750 × $0.0005 = $0.375. Escalations: 75 × $0.01 = $0.75. Large direct: 250 × $0.01 = $2.50. Total ≈ $3.63, against $10 before.
iv: How do you decide which requests can go to a small model?

Label a sample of real traffic, run both models, and check which requests the small model passes on your evals. Start with rules on task type and length, then train a router on outcome data, with validators so failures escalate.
What's the difference between a router and a cascade?

A router predicts up front and sends each request to one model. A cascade tries the cheap model first and escalates on failure or low confidence. Cascades need a reliable check and add latency on escalations; routers need a good predictor.
mis: Routing for cost without measuring quality per route
Track success rate per route and per request type
Escalating without a validator
Escalate on schema checks, confidence or a judge score

caching.t: Base input: $3 per million tokens. Cache write 1.25×, read 0.1×. A 20,000-token prefix is used on 10 calls within the cache window. What does the prefix cost with caching, in $?
caching.a: Without caching: 200,000 tokens × $3/M = $0.60. With caching: one write (20,000 × $3.75/M = $0.075) plus 9 reads (180,000 × $0.30/M = $0.054) = $0.129, about 78% less.
iv: What breaks prompt caching?

Any change before the cache breakpoint: timestamps, request IDs, reordered tools or examples, or per-user text in the system prompt. Keep the static prefix byte-identical and put variable content last.
How is prompt caching different from semantic caching?

Prompt caching reuses the processed prefix, and the model still generates a fresh answer. Semantic caching returns a stored answer for a similar question without calling the model: cheaper, but it risks stale or wrong answers.
mis: Putting the date or user name at the top of the system prompt
Move variable content to the end
Never checking cache usage
Monitor cache read and write tokens per request

controls.t: Steps use 4k, 5k, 6k, 7k, 8k, 9k, 10k and 11k tokens. You set a step budget of 5 and trim tool output so each step is 30% smaller. Total tokens after, in thousands?
controls.a: Before: 60k. After: the first five steps (4+5+6+7+8 = 30k) × 0.7 = 21k, about a third of the original.
iv: Why are agents so much more expensive than single LLM calls?

Each step resends the growing context, tool definitions and earlier tool outputs, so tokens compound across steps, and loops can run long. Step budgets, trimmed tool output and fewer loaded tools attack the compounding.
How do you choose max_tokens?
Measure the output-length distribution per task type on real traffic, set the cap a little above the 95th–99th percentile, and handle truncation gracefully.
mis: One global max_tokens for every task
Set caps per task type from measured lengths
Returning raw API payloads to the model
Return only the fields the next step needs

pruning.t: Context starts at 2k tokens and grows by 2k per turn, so turns 1–5 send 2k, 4k, 6k, 8k and 10k. If pruning caps every turn at 6k, what is the new total input, in thousands?
pruning.a: Before: 30k. After: 2 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24k. The saving grows with every extra turn.
iv: How do you prune without losing important information?

Keep recent turns word for word, summarize older ones into decisions, facts and open tasks, clear tool outputs once their key values are recorded, and keep durable facts in external memory the agent can query. Validate on long-task evals.
How does pruning interact with prompt caching?

Caching rewards a stable prefix, and pruning rewrites history, invalidating the cache after the change point. Prune in larger, less frequent steps and keep the system prompt and tools above the pruned region.
mis: Cutting from the start and losing the system prompt
Keep system prompt and tools; prune the middle
Summaries that drop open tasks
Keep decisions, facts and pending actions in every summary

scheduling.t: Interactive load peaks at 6 units. Background work adds 3 units per hour for 4 hours, currently during that peak. Move it to hours where interactive load is 1. What peak capacity do you now need?
scheduling.a: Peak drops from 6 + 3 = 9 to max(6, 1 + 3) = 6 units: a third less reserved capacity for the same work.
iv: How do you keep interactive latency low while heavy background jobs run?
Separate queues and worker pools, prioritize interactive traffic, schedule background work off-peak, and cap background concurrency so it can't use up shared rate limits.
Why use exponential backoff on retries?
Immediate retries during an outage or rate limit multiply load and cost. Backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s… with jitter) spreads them out, lets the provider recover and avoids synchronized retry storms.
mis: Retrying immediately in a tight loop
Exponential backoff with jitter and a retry cap
One shared rate limit for chat and batch jobs
Separate quotas and queues per workload

batch.t: 10,000 requests, each 1,500 input and 200 output tokens. Standard prices: $3/M input, $15/M output. What's the batch cost at 50% off, in $?
batch.a: Standard: 15M input × $3 = $45, plus 2M output × $15 = $30, total $75. Batch: $37.50.
iv: Which workloads fit batch APIs, and which don't?

Fit: anything nobody waits on, such as nightly tagging, evals, backfills and bulk summaries. Don't fit: interactive chat, agent loops that need each result before the next step, or jobs due within a few hours.
How do you handle partial failures in a batch?
Give every request a unique custom ID, record status per ID when results arrive, and resubmit only failed or expired IDs in a follow-up batch, with idempotent writes on your side.
mis: Running nightly jobs through the real-time API
Send anything nobody waits on through the batch API
Losing track of which item failed
Custom IDs and per-item status tracking

semcache.t: Tarang Mobile sends its 60,000 daily FAQ questions through a semantic cache; account questions skip it. 45,600 are hits. An LLM answer costs ₹0.40 and each lookup ₹0.01. How many rupees a day does the cache save?
semcache.a: Hits avoid 45,600 × ₹0.40 = ₹18,240 of LLM calls. Every FAQ question pays a lookup: 60,000 × ₹0.01 = ₹600. Net saving: ₹18,240 − ₹600 = ₹17,640 a day.
iv: How is a semantic response cache different from prompt caching?

Prompt caching is a provider feature: the processed prompt prefix is reused, but the model still generates a fresh answer, so answers stay correct and only input cost falls. A semantic cache sits in your own stack and returns a stored answer when a new question is similar enough, so the model is not called at all. It saves more per hit but can return a wrong answer on a near miss, a stale answer after the source changes, or another user's answer if scoped badly.
How would you choose the similarity threshold?

Build a labelled set from real traffic: paraphrase pairs that should share an answer and near misses that should not, such as two plans or two countries. Embed them with the cache's own model, and for each threshold measure recall and the false-hit rate. Pick the loosest threshold whose false-hit rate is acceptable, then keep sampling live hits for review, because traffic drifts.
mis: Caching every intent in one global cache
Exclude account-specific and live-data intents, and tag entries with a scope
Relying on TTL alone when source content changes
Tag entries with the source version and purge or stop matching when it changes

costattr.t: Invoice drafting spends ₹3,68,000 a month and drafts 2,62,857 invoices. What is the cost per invoice in ₹, to two decimals?
iv: How would you find out where an LLM bill goes?
Route every call through a gateway or wrapper that requires tags for team, feature, customer and run, reject untagged calls, and report spend and unit cost by tag.
How do you stop a runaway agent loop from costing a fortune?
Give each run a token or rupee budget checked before every call, stop gracefully with a clear message, alert at a share of the budget, and flag spend spikes per tag.
mis: One account-wide hard cap
Cap per run and per customer instead
Budgets in tokens across models with different prices
Budget in rupees using current prices

gloss: token
The unit models read and bill by; roughly three quarters of an English word on average.
SLM
Small language model: cheaper and faster, good for simple, well-defined tasks.
cascade
Trying a cheap model first and escalating to a stronger one only when a check fails.
cache hit rate
Share of input tokens served from the prompt cache instead of processed fresh.
cache breakpoint
The point up to which a prompt is cached; everything before it must be identical.
TTL
Time to live: how long a cached item stays available before it expires.
max_tokens
The cap on how many tokens a model may generate in one response.
step budget
The maximum number of iterations or tool calls an agent may take for one task.
context window
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider in one request.
exponential backoff
Retrying after increasing delays (1 s, 2 s, 4 s…) to avoid overloading a service.
batch API
An asynchronous API that processes many requests at a discount within a delivery window, often 24 hours.
provisioned throughput
Reserved model capacity paid for by time rather than per token.
semantic cache
A store of full answers keyed by the embedding of the question, so a new question similar enough to a cached one gets the stored answer without a model call.
false hit
A semantic-cache match that returns a stored answer to a question it does not fit, such as a UAE roaming answer for a USA roaming question.
cosine distance
One minus cosine similarity; a distance threshold of 0.10 is the same as requiring similarity of at least 0.90.
cache invalidation
Removing or retiring cached entries when the content they were built from changes, instead of waiting for them to expire.
cost attribution
Splitting spend by tags such as team, feature, customer and run.
unit cost
Spend per business outcome, such as ₹ per invoice or per resolved ticket.
run budget
A limit on tokens, rupees or steps for a single agent run.

caching.name: Prefix Caching
caching.note: Same idea at two levels: prompt caching is what the API provider offers; prefix caching is the KV-cache reuse inside the inference engine.

caching.name: Context Pruning
caching.note: Pruning rewrites the prompt prefix, which can cancel prompt-cache savings.

caching.name: Short-Term Memory and Compaction
caching.note: Every clear or compaction rewrites the prompt prefix, so clear in fewer, larger steps to protect the cache.

caching.name: System Prompt Design
caching.note: Stable system-prompt text first and variables last is what makes prompt caching work.

caching.name: Semantic Response Caching
caching.note: Prompt caching reuses the processed prompt prefix but the model still writes a fresh answer; a semantic cache skips the model and returns a stored answer, with the risk of false hits and stale replies.

caching.name: Long-Context Prompting
caching.note: Prompt caching turns a long shared document prefix from full price into a fraction on every later question.

pruning.name: Prompt Caching
pruning.note: Pruning rewrites the prompt prefix, which can cancel prompt-cache savings.

pruning.name: AST-Precise Localization
pruning.note: Loading only the needed code nodes is context pruning for coding agents.

pruning.name: Context Budgeting
pruning.note: Pruning cuts tokens to save money; context budgeting curates and orders them so accuracy holds at length.

pruning.name: Short-Term Memory and Compaction
pruning.note: Compaction is pruning with a rule about what must survive: IDs, amounts, decisions and open tasks.

routing.name: System-Level Eval
routing.note: Route traffic to a small model only after system-level eval shows it passes on that traffic.

routing.name: Speculative Decoding
routing.note: Both pair a small model with a large one: routing picks one per request, speculative decoding uses both on every step.

routing.name: Workflow Patterns
routing.note: Model routing picks which model answers by difficulty and cost; workflow routing picks which path (prompt, tools, steps) by request type. A route can also pick a smaller model.

routing.name: Reasoning Models and Thinking Budgets
routing.note: Routing by difficulty applies to effort levels too: low effort for routine requests, high for hard ones.

routing.name: Handoffs
routing.note: Routing picks a model for one request; a handoff moves ownership of the conversation, with its state, to another agent.

routing.name: Prompt and Model Versioning
routing.note: A routed system has one release per route: pin the snapshot for each model tier and version them together.

routing.name: Distillation into a Small Model
routing.note: A distilled student is only useful behind a router: easy, common queries go to the student and hard or low-confidence ones to the teacher.

routing.name: Realtime Voice Agents and Latency Budgets
routing.note: A fast, small model for the first reply keeps voice latency down; escalate hard turns to a larger one.

routing.name: Validation and Repair Loops
routing.note: When validation keeps failing on a small model, a cascade escalates that request to a larger one; tiering picks the cheapest model that passes each step.

routing.name: Prompting Reasoning Models
routing.note: Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it; for reasoning models that means lookups go to a non-reasoning model and only multi-step tasks pay for thinking.

routing.name: Latency Budgets and Streaming
routing.note: Using a faster model for early steps is model routing applied to latency: a small model classifies, the large one answers.

controls.name: Procedural Memory
controls.note: Reusing a proven procedure cuts steps, the biggest driver of agent token spend.

controls.name: ReAct Loop
controls.note: Step caps, compact tool results and fewer loaded tools are the controls that keep a ReAct loop affordable.

controls.name: Tool Interface Design
controls.note: Controls trim tool output for cost; tool design shapes names, results and errors so the model chooses and self-corrects.

controls.name: Failure Modes and Coordination Control
controls.note: Prompt and tool controls trim one agent’s usage; coordination control adds team-level caps on turns, tokens, time and depth.

controls.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI Tracing
controls.note: Token counts on every span show which steps and tools drive cost, the input for step caps and tool pruning.

controls.name: Tool Search and Large Tool Sets
controls.note: Loading fewer tool definitions per call is one of the biggest token savings; tool search does it without losing access to the rest.

controls.name: Cost Attribution and Budget Guards
controls.note: Step budgets cap one run's work; cost attribution adds rupee budgets and shows which runs hit them.

batch.name: Benchmark Suites
batch.note: Run large eval and benchmark suites through batch APIs at about half price.

semcache.name: Prompt Caching
semcache.note: Prompt caching reuses the processed prompt prefix but the model still writes a fresh answer; a semantic cache skips the model and returns a stored answer, with the risk of false hits and stale replies.

semcache.name: Semantic Embeddings
semcache.note: The cache matches questions by embedding similarity, so the embedding model decides which paraphrases and near misses land above the threshold.

semcache.name: HNSW Index
semcache.note: At scale the cached questions live in a vector index such as HNSW, so each lookup stays fast enough to be far cheaper than an LLM call.

semcache.name: PII Detection and Redaction
semcache.note: Answers that contain personal data must never enter a shared cache; the same detection used for redaction can keep them out.

costattr.name: Prompt & Tool Controls
costattr.note: Step budgets cap one run's work; cost attribution adds rupee budgets and shows which runs hit them.

costattr.name: Multi-Tenancy and Access Control
costattr.note: The tenant id used for data isolation is the same tag used for per-customer caps.

costattr.name: Incident Response and Trace Replay
costattr.note: Spend spikes by tag are an incident signal like error rates.

gifs.batch: 100,000 requests are written to a JSONL file with custom IDs, submitted to a batch API, matched back by ID with failed IDs resubmitted, and cost $375 instead of $750 in real time.
gifs.caching: A prompt is ordered with a 12,000-token static prefix before the question; over 20 calls the first writes the cache at 1.25× and the rest read it at 0.1×, cutting billed input from 244,000 to 41,800 base-price tokens, down 83%.
gifs.controls: A KYC agent task drops from 8 steps and 52k tokens to 4 steps and 11k tokens after loading 3 of 14 tools, capping replies, trimming tool output and setting a step budget, while the eval pass rate stays at 94%.
gifs.costattr: Every LLM call is tagged with feature, customer, run id and model. Spend bars grow by tag: GST invoices 46 percent, the support agent 31 percent, reconciliation runs 15 percent and one free-tier customer 8 percent. Guards on the same tags add a ₹50 budget per run, a ₹500 daily cap per customer and spike alerts, and monthly waste falls from ₹2,00,000 to ₹14,000.
gifs.pruning: Context per turn grows to 40k tokens without pruning, while summarizing whenever it passes 16k keeps it small, reducing input paid over turns 0 to 20 from 441k to 190k tokens.
gifs.routing: Ten labelled requests pass through a router: eight go to a small model and two to a large one, a validator escalates one failed small-model answer, and spend falls to 8 × 0.05 + 3 × 1.00 = 3.4, or 34% of sending everything to the large model.
gifs.scheduling: Background contract-note jobs move from the 16:00 peak to overnight hours, so the same 113 units of daily work need reserved capacity of 8 instead of 11 and utilization rises from 43% to 59%.
gifs.semcache: Animated scene for Semantic Response Caching at Tarang Mobile, a fictional telecom operator, with a 0.90 similarity threshold. On the left, four customer questions arrive. “Activate roaming?” scores 0.94 and “roaming kaise on kare?” scores 0.92 against the cached question “How do I turn on roaming?”, so both are hits. “What is my bill?” is marked as an account question and goes straight to the model. “Roaming packs for USA” scores 0.91 against the cached “Roaming packs for UAE” and is marked as a false hit. On the right, a global cache tagged tariff_v 09 holds three entries. Next the tariff page changes to version 10, and the cached “Price of the 299 plan” answer is struck through and purged, while a note says near misses are sampled for review. Finally two bars compare LLM calls a day: 1,00,000 with no cache and 54,400 with the semantic cache, saving ₹17,640 a day.

header.lede: Agent bills grow fast because agents loop, resend long prompts and default to the biggest model. Every technique here pulls one of three levers: fewer requests, fewer tokens per request, or a lower price per token.
